# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Standard place:** Cork, Munster, Ireland
- **Type:** County (formed 1606; boundaries were stable through the 1830s–1840s)
- **Administrative center:** Cork City
- **Province:** Munster
- **Population during period:** No population figures returned by the tools for this fixture. Historically, Cork was Ireland's largest county and one of its most populous; the Great Famine of 1845–1852 caused catastrophic population loss through death and emigration.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural (tenant farming, small holdings). Cork City and Cobh (Queenstown) were major commercial and port centres.
- **Religious composition:** Overwhelmingly Roman Catholic; a Protestant minority including Church of Ireland (Anglican) and Presbyterian congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine began in 1845, transforming emigration from a steady stream into a flood. Cobh (then called Queenstown) was Ireland's principal emigration port.

---

## Boundary Changes

County Cork was formed in 1606 and its boundaries were stable during the 1830s–1840s. There were no significant jurisdictional changes that would split records across different parent counties during this period. The county was subdivided internally into **baronies**, **civil parishes**, and **townlands** — the townland is the smallest and most genealogically useful unit; always try to identify your ancestor's specific townland, as records are often organised at that level.

---

## Available Record Types

### ⚠️ Civil Registration — **DOES NOT APPLY to this period**

- **Start date for births and deaths:** 1 January 1864
- **Start date for non-Catholic marriages:** 1845
- **Start date for Roman Catholic marriages:** 1 January 1864
- **Impact on your research:** There are **no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates** for anyone living in County Cork in the 1830s–1840s. Do not expect to find a civil registration document for this ancestor — use church records instead.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

### Church Records — **PRIMARY SOURCE for this period**

This is the most critical record type for the 1830s–1840s.

**Roman Catholic parishes**
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages (burials are rarely recorded in Catholic registers)
- **Survival:** Varies by parish. Many Cork RC parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s; some begin later or have gaps. Some parishes have no surviving pre-Famine registers.
- **Where held & access:** The **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** holds microfilm and digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880 and provides them **free online** at registers.nli.ie. This is your first stop for Cork Catholic parish records.
- **Digitization level:** Images available online (free); indexing varies by parish — some are name-searchable, others require browsing register by register.
- **Important note:** Identify your ancestor's specific civil parish and then the corresponding Catholic parish — they do not always align.

**Church of Ireland (Anglican)**
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes
- **Where held:** The **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)** in Dublin holds many Cork CofI registers; others remain in local parish custody. Some were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire (see Record Losses below).
- **Digitization level:** Partial — some are on FamilySearch microfilm; consult the RCBL directly for specific parishes.

**Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker**
- Smaller communities present in Cork, particularly in Cork City. Records vary in survival and accessibility; consult denominational archives.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

### Census Records — **SEVERELY LIMITED for this period**

- **Irish national census** was taken in 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 — but **nearly all pre-1901 returns were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire**. Only fragments of the 1821 and 1831 returns survive for any county, and survivals for Cork are minimal.
- **The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive** in full, but these post-date your ancestor's emigration.
- **Substitute sources** (see below) must be used in place of census records for the 1830s–1840s.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

### Census Substitutes — **CRITICAL for this period**

Because census returns were destroyed, two land/tax surveys function as the primary census substitutes:

**Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)**
- Lists occupiers of **tithe-liable agricultural land** across Ireland, including most of County Cork.
- Names the landholder, the townland, and the valuation of the land.
- **Coverage:** Covers the early 1830s for most Cork parishes — directly in your target window.
- **Limitations:** Lists only heads of household who occupied tithe-liable land. Landless labourers, cottiers, and town-dwellers may not appear.
- **Where held & access:** Available on FamilySearch and IrishGenealogy.ie; name-indexed and searchable online.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images online (free on IrishGenealogy.ie).

**Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork in the early 1850s)**
- Lists **every householder** in Ireland — far more comprehensive than the Tithe Books. Includes name, townland, lessor (landlord), and description of property.
- **Coverage:** Conducted county-by-county 1848–1864; Cork was completed around 1852 — just after the target window, making it ideal for tracking survivors and emigrants.
- **Where held & access:** Fully available and name-indexed on AskAboutIreland.ie (free) and Ancestry.com (subscription). Images and full text searchable.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images online.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

### Land Records

- **System:** Ireland used a **townland system** rather than a U.S.-style metes-and-bounds or rectangular survey. Land was held under lease from landlords; most Catholic tenants were **tenant farmers**, not freeholders.
- **Estate records:** Large landlord estates maintained their own rent rolls, maps, and tenant records. Survival varies; some are held by the **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)** and the **National Library of Ireland**.
- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin):** Registered leases and property transactions from 1708 onward. Cork leases from the 1830s–1840s may appear here if formally registered. Available at the Registry of Deeds in Dublin; some indexing available online.
- **Valuation Office:** Successor records to Griffith's Valuation tracking subsequent changes to tenancies — useful for tracing a family through the second half of the 19th century.
- **Note:** The tools did not surface specific digitized land record collections for County Cork at FamilySearch — consult the FamilySearch Wiki and the NAI directly for current digitization status.

---

### Probate and Wills

- **Pre-1858:** Wills were proved in Church of Ireland ecclesiastical courts (Prerogative Court and Consistorial Courts). For Cork, this was the **Consistorial Court of Cork and Ross** and the **Consistorial Court of Cloyne**.
- **⚠️ 1922 Fire Destruction:** Almost all original pre-1858 wills and many later ones were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire.
- **What survives:** **Indexes** to wills and administrations survived (the books of grants). Abstracts and copies of some wills appear in other collections (e.g., the Inland Revenue will registers, solicitors' copies). The **NAI** holds surviving will calendars from 1858 onward.
- **Digitization level:** Indexes are partially searchable online (Irish Will Calendars on Ancestry); original wills for this period are largely destroyed.
- **Practical advice:** Do not assume a pre-Famine ancestor left a will — most tenant farmers did not. Probate was largely a Protestant landowning-class record type for this period.

---

### Emigration Records — **HIGH VALUE for your research**

- **Cork ports:** Cobh (Queenstown) and Cork City were Ireland's primary emigration ports, particularly during and after the Famine (mid-1840s onward). Emigrants in the late 1830s–early 1840s also departed from Cork.
- **Passenger manifests (arrival records):** Record every person aboard ship, **including infants and young children traveling with parents** — not just heads of household. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members. These are held primarily at NARA (U.S.) and are indexed and searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **Departure records:** Irish port departure records for this period are sparse. Arrival records in the destination country (U.S., Canada, Australia, UK) are the main source.
- **Famine-era ships:** The period 1845–1852 produced the largest volume of records. Pre-Famine emigration (1830s–early 1840s) is less well documented but manifests exist.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

### Poor Law Records

- The Irish Poor Law Act of 1838 established **Poor Law Unions** across Ireland, each with a workhouse. County Cork had multiple unions (e.g., Cork, Bandon, Fermoy, Kanturk, Kinsale, Macroom, Midleton, Mallow, Millstreet, Skibbereen, etc.).
- **Record types:** Workhouse admission and discharge registers, indoor relief lists, outdoor relief lists, Poor Law rate books.
- **Relevance:** From 1838 onward — overlaps the later part of your target window and the Famine period. These records can document the poorest families who may not appear in land records.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland; survival is uneven by union.
- **Digitization level:** The tools did not surface specific digitized Poor Law collections — consult NAI and local archive finding aids.

---

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1798 Rebellion, the 1803 Emmet Rebellion, and British Army service are the main military contexts for men from Cork in this era.
- **British Army:** Many Irishmen served in the British Army. Service records, pension records, and muster rolls are held at The National Archives (UK), Kew. Fold3 (subscription) and FindMyPast hold some British military records online.
- **Militia:** Local militia records from the late 18th–early 19th century; survival is sparse.
- **Note:** The external_links_search returned Fold3 as a curated resource for this place — it is the primary online database for British military records of the period.

---

### Newspapers

- **Cork Examiner** (founded 1841) and the **Cork Constitution** (founded 1822) are the major Cork newspapers for this period. They published marriage notices, death notices, legal announcements, and emigration news.
- **Where held:** The **British Newspaper Archive** (subscription, findmypast.co.uk), the **Irish Newspaper Archive** (subscription), and the **National Library of Ireland** hold Cork papers for this period.
- **Newspapers.com** was returned as a curated resource by the external_links_search; it has some Irish newspaper content but coverage is more limited than the Irish Newspaper Archive.
- **Value:** Death and marriage notices in Cork newspapers can substitute for missing civil records, particularly for middle-class and Protestant families. Catholic tenant farmers are less likely to appear.

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) was returned as a curated resource. It has partial coverage of Irish cemeteries, typically transcribed by volunteers — coverage is uneven.
- **Gravestone transcriptions:** Local heritage societies in Cork have transcribed many graveyards; these are often held by the **Cork County Library** or published in journals of the **Cork Historical and Archaeological Society**.
- **Digitization level:** Partial online coverage (Find A Grave); physical transcription records held locally.

---

### Tax Records (Beyond Tithe Books)

- **Hearth Money Rolls** (17th century) and earlier tax lists predate your window.
- **Flattened valuation books / cancelled land books:** Post-Griffith's records at the Valuation Office tracking changes to tenancies — useful for tracing families after they appear in Griffith's.
- **Poor Law Rate Books:** Rate (tax) assessment rolls for each Poor Law Union, listing ratepayers by townland — can substitute for later census years.

---

---

## Records NOT Online (or Only Partially Online)

- **Church of Ireland parish registers** for many Cork parishes — still in local custody or at the RCBL; not all are digitised or on FamilySearch.
- **Poor Law workhouse registers** — held at NAI; not comprehensively digitised.
- **Estate records and rent rolls** — held at NLI and NAI; finding aids available but records themselves largely require in-person access.
- **Registry of Deeds transcripts** — partial online indexes only; the full memorial books require in-person or transcription requests.
- **Wills and probate records** — mostly destroyed (see below); surviving abstracts and copies scattered across various archives.
- **Cork newspapers pre-1841** — limited online coverage; NLI and Cork County Library hold physical/microfilm copies.

---

## Known Record Losses ⚠️

**The 1922 Four Courts Fire — the defining catastrophe for Irish genealogy**

On 30 June 1922, during the Irish Civil War, the Public Record Office of Ireland in the Four Courts, Dublin, was destroyed by fire and explosion. This is the single greatest record loss in Irish genealogical history. What was destroyed includes:

- **Nearly all pre-1901 Irish census returns** (1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871, 1881, 1891) — almost nothing survives for County Cork
- **Most pre-1858 Church of Ireland parish registers** deposited with the PRO
- **The majority of pre-1858 wills and testamentary records**
- **Many government and administrative records**

**What survived or was never at risk:**
- Catholic parish registers (held by parishes and the NLI, not the PRO)
- Tithe Applotment Books (survived)
- Griffith's Valuation (survived)
- Registry of Deeds records (held at a separate building)
- Church of Ireland registers still in parish custody

The destruction of the 1841 and 1851 censuses is particularly painful for Famine-era research. Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books are the essential substitutes.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Genealogy Records")*

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records, not civil registration.** Civil registration did not exist for this period. Your first search should be the appropriate Catholic or Church of Ireland parish register via the NLI (free online). Know your ancestor's townland if possible — it identifies the civil parish, which maps to the church parish.

2. **Identify the townland.** The townland is Ireland's smallest administrative unit and the key to unlocking records. Every Irish record — Tithe Books, Griffith's Valuation, church registers, estate records — is organised by townland. Use Griffith's Valuation to establish the townland, then work backward.

3. **Work Griffith's Valuation as a census substitute.** Published for Cork circa 1852, it lists every householder. It's your best comprehensive snapshot of who was there just after the Famine. Cross-reference with the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) to see who was in the same household location a generation earlier.

4. **Use Catholic parish registers with caution about gaps.** Many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, but survival is uneven. A missing baptism may mean the register doesn't survive, not that the event didn't occur. The NLI website lists the date ranges for each surviving Cork register — check this before concluding a record is absent.

5. **Track the emigration voyage.** For Famine-era departures (1845 onward), Cork/Cobh manifests are relatively well preserved. Pre-Famine departures (1830s–early 1840s) are patchier. Search arrival records in the U.S. (Ancestry, FamilySearch), Canada (Library and Archives Canada), and Australia (National Archives of Australia) based on the destination known from family tradition. The full manifest lists all family members, including children — don't search only for the head of household.

6. **Don't overlook the four-stage record sequence:** Tithe Applotment Books (1820s–1830s) → Church records (baptism/marriage) → Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s) → Poor Law records (1838+). Working these four sources together builds a family picture despite the census destruction.

7. **For Protestant ancestors,** Church of Ireland registers and the RCBL are essential. CofI registers tend to have better survival than Catholic ones for the early 19th century, and they recorded burials as well as baptisms and marriages.

8. **Wills are largely a dead end** for Catholic tenant farmers in this period — don't invest heavily in probate research unless you have evidence of property ownership. Wills that do survive are largely for Protestant and landed families.

9. **Newspapers are more useful than often assumed** for middle-class families: the Cork Examiner (founded 1841) and Cork Constitution published marriage and death notices. Search the Irish Newspaper Archive and British Newspaper Archive.

10. **Poor Law records (from 1838)** can document the most impoverished families — landless labourers, cottiers — who are invisible in the Tithe Books and may appear only fleetingly in Griffith's Valuation.

---

*This guide is based on the FamilySearch Wiki "Ireland Genealogy Records" article and place data from the FamilySearch place database. For current digitization status of specific County Cork collections, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/wiki and the National Archives of Ireland (nationalarchives.ie).*

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, created from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** No figures returned by the population tool; consult U.S. decennial census totals. Population grew rapidly driven by anthracite coal extraction.

- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (large Irish-born congregation), Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal, Welsh Calvinist Methodist. German Lutheran and Reformed churches kept records in German.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid anthracite development (1840s–1870s), Civil War (1861–1865), Molly Maguires labor unrest (late 1860s–1876 trials), railroad expansion throughout the period.

---

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. **Boundaries were stable throughout the entire 1840–1880 research window** — no boundary changes affect which county's records apply.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, created from Berks and Northampton counties (FamilySearch place record, dateRange +1811/)
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this fixture. Consult U.S. decennial census totals. Population grew rapidly during this period driven by anthracite coal extraction.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry; related industries included iron/steel manufacturing, the Schuylkill Canal (active through the 1870s), and railroads. Pottsville was the commercial center.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigration (especially post-1845 Famine), Welsh and English miners, German settlers, and (later in the period) the beginning of Eastern European immigration. This ethnic mix directly shapes what church denominations are present and what languages records are written in.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (large Irish-born congregation), Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal, Welsh Calvinist Methodist. German Lutheran and Reformed churches kept records in German.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid anthracite development (1840s–1870s), Civil War service (1861–1865), Molly Maguires labor unrest (late 1860s–1876 trials), railroad expansion throughout the period.

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. Boundaries were stable throughout the entire 1840–1880 research window — no boundary changes affect which county's records apply.
- **Pre-1811 records:** Any events before 1811 in this territory are recorded under Berks or Northampton County, not Schuylkill.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania enacted statewide civil registration of births and deaths in 1893. **No civil birth or death records exist for 1840–1880.**
- **Marriages:** County-level marriage registers may exist at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, but the only digitized FamilySearch marriage volume for Schuylkill begins in 1870 (see Marriage Records below). Marriages 1840–1869 must be sought in church records or at the courthouse.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials) are the primary substitute for births and deaths throughout this entire period.

### Church records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985" (collection ID 1401638) — 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images. Covers the full target period and includes Schuylkill County congregations. **Digitization: indexed + images** (name-searchable; free on FamilySearch).
- **FamilySearch Schuylkill-specific volume:** Image group 007936751 — Church Records 1842–1895, 187 images. Languages: English and German. **Digitization: browse-only** (0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image-by-image; German-language entries require reading the original.
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal, Welsh Calvinist Methodist. Each immigrant community (Irish, German, Welsh) maintained separate congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Local parishes, diocesan archives (Catholic Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill County Catholic parishes), denominational repositories, FamilySearch.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Available for 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 (all within the target period). The 1850 Schuylkill County census is indexed on Ancestry (external link returned by tools). All federal census years are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. **Digitization: indexed + images.**
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules list persons who died in the year preceding each census: 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 schedules exist. With no civil death registration before 1893, these schedules are critical for identifying deaths in the coal-mining context.
- **Pennsylvania state census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Veteran schedules:** The 1890 federal census includes a Union veteran schedule (just outside target period); the 1880 census does not have a separate veterans schedule but does record Civil War service status.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch Pennsylvania-level collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196) — 2,304,118 images. Note: personCount is 0 and imageCount equals recordCount, indicating this is an image collection; the Schuylkill-specific probate volume (below) confirms 0% indexing for this county. **Digitization: browse-only images.**
- **FamilySearch Schuylkill-specific volume:** Image group 007936749 — Probate Records 1851–1930, 412 images. **Digitization: browse-only** (0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). Coverage begins 1851; probate from before 1851 not in this volume.
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate settlements.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills (Pottsville); older records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Naturalization records

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill-specific volume:** Image group 007936750 — Naturalization Records 1849–1915, 298 images. **Digitization: browse-only** (0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). Covers most of the target period; begins 1849.
- **Important:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — not only federal courts. Also check Quarter Sessions court records locally and NARA for federal court filings.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse; NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) for federal court records.

### Land records

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill-specific volume:** Image group 007936752 — Deed Records 1815–1900, 543 images, **partially indexed** (22% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). The most accessible land record set digitally; search by name for the 22% indexed, then browse the remainder.
- **System:** Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds (state-land) state. Deeds describe land by courses and distances with named adjoining owners — not the federal township-range-section system.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, sheriff's deeds (common in a mining county with debt), mechanics' liens.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville.

### Marriage records

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill-specific volume:** Image group 007936753 — Marriage Records 1870–1910, 94 images. **Digitization: browse-only** (0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). Coverage begins 1870 only.
- **Gap:** No digitized FamilySearch marriage records for Schuylkill County 1840–1869. Search the statewide church records collection (1401638) and contact the County Courthouse for this gap.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Orphans' Court / clerk of courts, Pottsville; church registers.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and Civil War (1861–1865).
- **Civil War:** Pennsylvania contributed heavily to the Union; many Schuylkill County men served. Service records and pension files are held at NARA (National Archives and Records Administration); the NARA Mid-Atlantic Region in Philadelphia is the nearest facility.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for earlier conflicts), draft registrations (1863 Civil War draft), muster rolls.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg):** Holds Pennsylvania adjutant general records, including Civil War regimental rosters and muster rolls for Pennsylvania units.
- **Online:** Fold3 and Ancestry have indexed Civil War pension and service records. No Schuylkill-specific military volumes appeared in the FamilySearch volume_search results — this is a gap.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover many Schuylkill County cemeteries; neither appeared as a curated external link in the FamilySearch results for this place/period, so full indexing extent is not confirmed from tool results.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, burial registers, and historical cemetery surveys may be held by local churches, the Historical Society of Schuylkill County, or the Pottsville Free Public Library.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Schuylkill County had active newspapers throughout this period, most notably the *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville), one of the most important newspapers in the anthracite region. Papers published legal notices, obituaries, marriage announcements, and mining accident reports (valuable given the industry).
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank index Pennsylvania historical newspapers; neither appeared in the FamilySearch curated external links for this place/period. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project may also hold partial runs.
- **Physical access:** The Pottsville Free Public Library and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County hold local newspaper collections on microfilm.

### Tax records

- **Target period:** County-level tax records (property, personal property) exist in Pennsylvania for 1840–1880. The only FamilySearch curated external link for tax records is "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" on Ancestry — outside the target window and not useful for 1840–1880.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists can confirm residence in intercensal years and are especially useful when other records are absent.

### Occupational records (anthracite coal mining)

- **Distinctive to this locality:** Schuylkill County's anthracite industry created occupational records not found in agricultural counties: mine employment rolls, accident and coroner's records from mine disasters, company store ledgers, union records (post-1869 Workingmen's Benevolent Association).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton); Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville). These records are generally physical only.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1800 (Before Statehood)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

In 1800 **Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction**. Your ancestor lived in one of several overlapping colonial and territorial regimes, each producing its own records:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | **French colonial** | France controlled Mobile Bay and interior; records in France |
| 1763–1780 | **British West Florida** | Britain administered the region |
| 1780–1813 | **Spanish colonial (Mobile District)** | Spain retook Mobile; held coastal area until U.S. forces occupied it in 1813 |
| **1798–1817** | **Mississippi Territory** | ← **Your primary jurisdiction at 1800**; covered all of present-day AL + MS |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Split off when western half became the state of Mississippi |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Statehood 14 December 1819 |

**At c. 1800**, your ancestor lived in the **Mississippi Territory**. County formation was still sparse — Washington County was organized in 1800; Madison County not until 1808. Records will be filed under "Mississippi Territory" and its early counties, **not** "Alabama." Search both Alabama-scoped and Mississippi-scoped FamilySearch collections, because territorial records appear under either.

---

## Primary Repositories

### 1. Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)
**Montgomery, Alabama** — [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov)

The single most important repository for pre-statehood Alabama research. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records"), ADAH holds:
- **Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** — the most important population substitutes for 1800
- Territorial **land records and grants**
- **Militia rolls** for present-day Alabama
- **Tax lists** (essential census substitutes for 1800–1819)
- Early county court records and probate files

### 2. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
**Washington, D.C. / Southeast Region (Atlanta)** — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)

- **1800 federal census for Mississippi Territory** — covers present-day Alabama (incomplete for this sparsely settled area)
- War of 1812 **service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants** — many Alabama-area men served
- **Federal land patents** — Alabama is a public-land (federal) state; original entries issued by the U.S. General Land Office

### 3. BLM General Land Office (GLO)
**Online** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)

Alabama's original landowners received federal patents, searchable free online. First Alabama land surveys began ca. 1806–1810, so the earliest patents date just after 1800 — prime evidence for the first wave of American settlers.

### 4. Archivo General de Indias *(Mobile-area ancestors)*
**Seville, Spain** — For ancestors in or near **Mobile before 1813**

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records"), Spanish records of the Mobile District include:
- Census returns
- Catholic church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials)
- Land grants

Copies of many Spanish records are held at the **Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.**

### 5. Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer & Mobile Municipal Archives *(French-era Mobile)*
**Aix-en-Provence, France** | Microfilm copies at **Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL**

For ancestors in the Mobile area during the French period (1702–1763), French colonial registers are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records")*

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 🗳️ Census & Population Substitutes
- **1800 federal census (Mississippi Territory)**: At NARA; on Ancestry and FamilySearch — covers present-day Alabama, but population was sparse and coverage incomplete
- **Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810**: Held at ADAH; some names indexed in FamilySearch coll. 2016756 (index only, no images)
- **Tax lists**: ADAH holds pre-statehood tax lists — the single most useful census substitute for the years between enumerations

### 🌍 Land Records *(highest priority for 1800)*
- **Federal land patents**: BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable online; earliest Alabama entries ca. 1806–1815
- **Territorial land grants**: FamilySearch Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records (coll. 1919694, from 1798); originals at ADAH and NARA
- **Spanish land grants** (Mobile area, pre-1813): Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress — **not on FamilySearch**
- **Tax/property lists**: ADAH — important for establishing residence when no census exists

### 📜 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **No civil registration** of births or deaths in Alabama until **1908**. For 1800, vital events exist only in church records or substitute sources.
- **Marriages**: County registers begin only after county formation. FamilySearch Alabama County Marriages (coll. 1598408) starts 1809; earlier marriages may be in court order books at ADAH
- **Church records**: Catholic registers in Mobile predate American settlement by generations. Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations were establishing records by the early 1800s. FamilySearch: Alabama Church Records (coll. 1986396, from 1803) and Mississippi Church Records (coll. 2034891, from 1800)

### ⚖️ Probate & Court Records
- **Alabama Probate Records** (coll. 1537764): 438,210 records, 219,105 images — earliest from 1809; county originals at ADAH
- **Mississippi County Court Records** (coll. 1855293): 245,670 records, from 1799 — may contain Alabama-area territorial records
- Territorial-level court records: ADAH and NARA (Southeast Region)

### ⚔️ Military Records
- **War of 1812 service and pension files**: NARA; Fold3 and Ancestry for digitized access — many Alabama settlers served
- **Mississippi Territory militia rolls**: ADAH — key for 1800–1815 period
- **Creek War 1813–1814 volunteers**: NARA service records

### ⛪ Church Records
- **Catholic (Mobile Diocese)**: Registers of baptism, marriage, and burial predate American control; at the Diocese of Mobile archives and partially in Spanish colonial archives
- **Protestant (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian)**: Congregations active in interior Alabama by the early 1800s; FamilySearch coll. 1986396 (from 1803)

### 📰 Newspapers
- Early Alabama newspapers begin ca. 1813; very limited coverage for exactly 1800. Chronicling America (Library of Congress, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) and Newspapers.com hold early regional papers

### 🪦 Cemetery Records
- FindAGrave (findagrave.com) for transcriptions; county historical and genealogical societies hold physical survey records

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No "Alabama" records exist for 1800** — the state didn't exist. All records from this period will be filed under "Mississippi Territory" or one of its early counties. Search both Alabama- and Mississippi-scoped FamilySearch collections as one connected research trail.

2. **County formation was incomplete** — Washington County was organized in 1800; Madison County not until 1808; many others later. If the county your ancestor lived in hadn't yet been formed, records will be at the territorial (or parent-county) level.

3. **No civil vital records** — Alabama did not require statewide birth or death registration until 1908. Church records and substitute sources (tax lists, territorial censuses, probate) are the primary vital-event proxies for c. 1800.

4. **Mobile-area ancestors need colonial archives** — the Mobile District was under Spanish administration until 1813. Vital records there are in Catholic church registers and Spanish colonial archives, not American government records. Start with the Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress copies.

5. **The 1800 federal census for Mississippi Territory** covered present-day Alabama but with incomplete enumeration given sparse settlement. Look for the ancestor under "Mississippi Territory," not Alabama.

6. **Tax lists are your best census substitute** — ADAH holds territorial tax lists that fill the gaps between the 1800 and 1810 federal censuses and the sparse territorial enumerations.

7. **FamilySearch territorial scope quirk** — querying "Mississippi Territory" on FamilySearch resolves to Mississippi state scope. When searching, try both "Alabama" and "Mississippi" as the place filter to ensure you catch all relevant territorial collections.

---

## Useful Societies & Further Resources

- **Alabama Department of Archives and History** — [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov)
- **Alabama Genealogical Society** — [algensoc.org](http://www.algensoc.org)
- **Mobile Genealogical Society** — especially important for Mobile-area / colonial research
- **FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy**: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy)
- **BLM GLO land patents**: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Chronicling America** (early newspapers): [chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)

---

**Bottom line for 1800 research**: Begin at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** for territorial tax lists and militia rolls (the best census substitutes for exactly 1800), then layer in the FamilySearch Mississippi territorial land records (from 1798), the federal census for Mississippi Territory, and — if your ancestor was near Mobile — the Spanish colonial records at the Library of Congress or the Archivo General de Indias.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, before 1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **First European settlement** | Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas), established 1686 by Henri de Tonti for France — first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley |
| **French colonial period** | Pre-1763 — governed as French Louisiana (La Louisiane), administered from New Orleans |
| **Spanish colonial period** | 1763–1800 — after the Treaty of Paris ending the Seven Years' War, France ceded all Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain; the region became part of the Spanish Province of Louisiana |
| **Return to France** | 1800 — Treaty of San Ildefonso; Spain secretly cedes Louisiana back to France |
| **U.S. acquisition** | 1803 — Louisiana Purchase |
| **U.S. territorial/state** | Territory of Arkansas 1819; State of Arkansas 1836 |
| **Population** | No formal population data survives for this period. European settlement was extremely sparse — Arkansas Post was a small military garrison and trading post; total European settlers in the Arkansas district numbered in the low hundreds at most. |
| **Economy** | Fur trade, military garrison, small-scale subsistence agriculture, trade with Native American tribes (primarily the Quapaw) |
| **Ethnic composition** | French Canadian and French Creole settlers, Spanish military and administrative personnel, Anglo-American traders arriving toward end of period; Quapaw and other Native American peoples |
| **Religion** | Exclusively Roman Catholic among European settlers; French Catholic missionaries present from the 1690s onward |

## Boundary changes

- **Before 1763:** Part of **French Louisiana** — no county-level subdivisions; all governed from New Orleans under French colonial law.
- **1763–1800:** Part of the **Spanish Province of Louisiana**, governed from New Orleans. The Arkansas district was administered as the **Post of Arkansas (Poste de Arkansas / El Puerto de Arkansas)** — a single civil-military district, not subdivided into counties or parishes.
- There are no county-level records for this period. The first U.S.-era county structure in Arkansas did not exist until after 1819.
- **Critical research implication:** Do not search Arkansas county courthouses for pre-1800 records. The relevant records are at Spanish colonial archives in Seville, at the Arkansas History Commission, and at the Library of Congress — not in any county-level repository.

---

## Available record types

### Church records ⭐ Primary vital record source

No civil registration existed during this period. Catholic sacramental registers are the only systematic record of births (baptisms), marriages, and burials.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. French missionaries (Jesuits, later secular clergy) served Arkansas Post from the early 1700s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials — covering both European settlers and, in many registers, Native Americans.
- **French-era registers (pre-1763):** French Catholic sacramental registers from Arkansas Post survive from the early 1700s, recording baptisms, marriages, and burials of settlers and Native Americans. According to the FamilySearch Wiki article *Arkansas Genealogy*, these are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission**.
- **Spanish-era registers (1763–1800) — digitized but browse-only:**

> **FamilySearch Image Group 008814402** — *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)*, Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, 1763–1800. **64 images.**
> - Digitization level: **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable
> - Language: **Spanish** (18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting)
> - Must be browsed page by page; no name search available
> - Free access at FamilySearch.org — search by image group number 008814402

**This is the only digitized FamilySearch holding for pre-1800 Arkansas.**

### Census records / Padrones

- **What exists:** The Spanish colonial government conducted periodic **padrones** (household censuses) of the Arkansas Post district. These listed heads of household, household members, sometimes ages and occupations — making them a valuable substitute for vital records.
- **Where held:**
  - **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock (transcriptions and copies)
  - **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain — *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* section (the primary Spanish colonial archive for Louisiana including Arkansas)
  - **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. — microfilm copies of Louisiana colonial documents, including some padrones
- **FamilySearch coverage:** The closest FamilySearch indexed collection is *Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870* (collection 2085124) — this begins in 1819 and does **not** cover the pre-1800 period. **No indexed census material exists on FamilySearch for pre-1800 Arkansas.**
- **Access:** Physical and microfilm only; not name-indexed online.

### Land records ⭐ Key substitute source

Land concession records are among the most genealogically rich documents for this period. Spanish colonial governors issued land grants (concesiones) to settlers; after the Louisiana Purchase, U.S. land commissioners required all claimants to document their Spanish or French grants — creating detailed claim files that effectively summarize a family's history in the Spanish period.

- **System:** Spanish land concession system
- **Where held:**
  - **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville (*Papeles de Cuba*)
  - **Arkansas History Commission** (copies and transcripts)
  - **NARA** — U.S. Board of Land Commissioners adjudication files for pre-1803 Spanish and French claims; these post-1803 claim files often name ancestors, describe original concessions, and give family history
  - **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) — some confirmed Spanish-era patents are digitized here
- **Access:** Archivo de Indias is physical in Seville; partially accessible via **PARES** (Portal de Archivos Españoles, pares.mcu.es — free, partial digitization). NARA land claim files are physical. BLM-GLO is free online.

### Military records

- **What exists:** Spanish garrison records for Arkansas Post — muster rolls, officer reports, and administrative correspondence. The garrison was small; records are part of the broader Louisiana colonial archive.
- **Where held:** **Archivo General de Indias** (Papeles de Cuba); some microfilm at the **Library of Congress**; **NARA** (for post-1803 U.S.-era military records only)
- **Access:** Physical in Seville; some microfilm at Library of Congress.

### Probate and court records

- **What exists:** Spanish colonial courts at Arkansas Post handled probate and civil matters for settlers who died in the district. Records are sporadic and survival is uncertain for the Arkansas district specifically.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Papeles de Cuba) and Arkansas History Commission.
- **Access:** Physical only; no digitized index for this period.

### Tax and fiscal records

- **What exists:** Some Spanish fiscal records (trade licensing, levies) exist as part of Louisiana Province administrative files.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias.
- **Access:** Physical only.

### Cemetery records

- **What exists:** Burials at Arkansas Post were recorded in the Catholic sacramental registers (see above). No separate sexton records are known to survive for this period.
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have very limited pre-1800 Arkansas entries.

### Newspaper records

- **What exists:** None. No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region during the Spanish colonial period. The nearest newspapers were in New Orleans and are of limited direct use for Arkansas settler research.

### Immigration records

- **What exists:** No formal immigration records. Arrival of settlers was noted in Spanish administrative correspondence and padrones. Anglo-American settlers arriving from the U.S. after ~1790 may appear in Spanish land concession petitions.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Holdings for pre-1800 Arkansas | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 1 browse-only image volume: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers 1763–1800, 64 images, in Spanish (image group 008814402). **No indexed collections.** | Free |
| **PARES** (pares.mcu.es) | Partial digitization of Archivo General de Indias holdings, including some Papeles de Cuba documents for Louisiana/Arkansas | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Some Spanish-era land patents confirmed post-1803 | Free |
| **ANOM** (anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr) | French colonial archives (Archives nationales d'outre-mer) — relevant for pre-1763 French Louisiana records | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR 72201 | Transcriptions and microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records, French Catholic registers, padrones; primary in-state repository for colonial-era research | In-person; finding aids at arkansasheritage.com |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | French Catholic sacramental registers from Arkansas Post (pre-1763 and possibly Spanish period); contact Diocese Archives | By appointment |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for Louisiana Province — *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* section covers Arkansas: padrones, land grants, military records, court records, correspondence | In-person in Seville; partial digitization on PARES |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of Louisiana colonial documents including some Arkansas Post records; WPA-era typed transcripts of colonial documents | Reading room; catalog at loc.gov |
| **NARA** (College Park, MD / Washington, D.C.) | U.S. Board of Land Commissioners files adjudicating pre-1803 Spanish/French claims; early Arkansas territorial records post-1803 | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Newberry Library**, Chicago | Strong French and Spanish colonial America holdings; Louisiana research resources | In-person; some digitized finding aids |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Louisiana State Museum, New Orleans) | French colonial Louisiana records relevant to the pre-1763 period | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for pre-1800 Arkansas but are **not** in any searchable online database:

- Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) for Arkansas Post — held at Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission
- Spanish land concession original documents — Archivo General de Indias, Papeles de Cuba
- Spanish colonial court and probate records — Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish military muster rolls and correspondence for Arkansas Post — Archivo General de Indias
- French Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763) — Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission
- WPA transcriptions of Louisiana colonial records — Library of Congress (physical only)

**The sole partial exception:** FamilySearch image group 008814402 (Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800) is online but is browse-only, in Spanish, with no name index.

---

## Known record losses

- The settlement at Arkansas Post was always small, so records were never abundant to begin with.
- Much of what was created in the Spanish period was sent to New Orleans or Seville — very little remained locally — and what survived is largely in the Archivo General de Indias.
- Some records were lost during the chaotic transfer of power from Spain → France → U.S. (1800–1803), but the Seville archive preserved the bulk of the administrative record.
- The Arkansas History Commission's colonial holdings are generally considered intact for what was transferred there, though coverage of the Arkansas district is inherently thin given the small population.

---

## Research tips

1. **Begin at the Arkansas History Commission.** It is the primary U.S. access point for colonial Arkansas research and holds transcriptions and microfilm of Seville documents. Contact them and review their finding aids before planning a trip to Spain. Website: arkansasheritage.com.

2. **The Archivo General de Indias (Papeles de Cuba) is the mother lode.** Spanish colonial records for Louisiana — including the Arkansas Post district — are organized in the *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* section. Check the **PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es) first: it is free, partially digitized, and may surface relevant documents without requiring a trip to Seville.

3. **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402 page by page.** The 64-image Arkansas Post sacramental register volume (1763–1800) is the only FamilySearch holding for this period. There is no name index — you must browse every image. The records are in 18th-century Spanish; consider engaging a genealogist with Spanish colonial paleography experience.

4. **Land claim adjudication files are a gold mine.** After 1803, the U.S. required everyone holding land under a Spanish or French grant to document their claim before commissioners. These NARA files often include the original concession date, the grantee's family history, and sworn depositions from neighbors — effectively creating a genealogical record of the Spanish period that survived when other documents did not.

5. **French-period research (pre-1763) requires different archives.** Before 1763 look to French Louisiana colonial records: the **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) and the French overseas colonial archives (**ANOM**, Aix-en-Provence, partly digitized at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr). The FamilySearch Wiki article *Arkansas Genealogy* (at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy) provides further guidance.

6. **The population was tiny — secondary literature may reconstruct it.** The entire pool of pre-1800 European settlers in Arkansas is small enough that published genealogical and historical works have substantially reconstructed it from colonial sources. Consult Morris Arnold's scholarship on colonial Arkansas law and settlement, which draws directly from the Seville archive records and can orient your research before you access original documents.

7. **All records for this period are in French or Spanish.** French (pre-1763) or Spanish (1763–1800) language skills — and familiarity with 18th-century script — are required to use original sources. Plan accordingly.

8. **After 1803, the research strategy changes completely.** The U.S. territorial period (Arkansas Territory established 1819, state 1836) produces American-style county records accessible through normal genealogical channels. The earliest FamilySearch-indexed collection for the territory is *Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870* (collection 2085124). Use that as your bridge from colonial research into the U.S. period.

---

**Summary of digitization levels for this period:**

| Record type | Digitization level |
|---|---|
| Catholic sacramental registers, 1763–1800 (Arkansas Post) | Browse-only images (FamilySearch, in Spanish) |
| Catholic sacramental registers, pre-1763 (French period) | Physical/microfilm — Diocese of Little Rock & AHC |
| Spanish padrones (household censuses) | Physical only — Archivo General de Indias & AHC |
| Spanish land concessions | Physical / partial PARES digitization |
| U.S. land claim adjudication files (post-1803, documenting Spanish grants) | Physical — NARA |
| Spanish military & court records | Physical only — Archivo General de Indias |
| No indexed online collections exist for pre-1800 Arkansas | — |

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (circa 1790, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Status in 1790:** Ohio did not yet exist. The region formed part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. That ordinance covered present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.
- **First county organized:** Washington County (1788), which initially covered the entire Northwest Territory east of the Scioto River and beyond.
- **Second county organized:** Hamilton County (1790), covering the southwestern corner of present-day Ohio including the Cincinnati area.
- **Statehood:** Ohio became the first state carved from the Northwest Territory on 1 March 1803.
- **Administrative center (territorial era):** Marietta, Ohio (Washington County seat; site of the first permanent American settlement in the territory).
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, land speculation, fur trade, early river commerce on the Ohio River.
- **Ethnic/Settlement composition:** Predominantly migrants from Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, New England (Connecticut Western Reserve settlers), and New Jersey; also Revolutionary War veterans claiming bounty land.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker congregations were among the earliest established. Catholic missions existed in some areas.
- **Key historical events:** Indian Wars (Battle of Fallen Timbers, 1794; Treaty of Greenville, 1795), which drove much of the settlement activity and produced military records.

---

## Boundary Changes

This is the core complexity for 1790 research, and involves **both temporal and geographic splits** — the two kinds behave very differently.

### Temporal split (sequential jurisdictions covering the same ground)
- **Before 1788:** No formal county government; any legal acts were under the broader Northwest Territory administration.
- **1788 onward:** Washington County governed essentially all of present-day Ohio. Records created here are at the Ohio History Connection, Columbus.
- **1790 onward:** Hamilton County split off to cover southwestern Ohio. Which county applies depends on where within Ohio the event occurred.
- **1790s–1803:** Additional counties were rapidly carved out (Ross, Adams, Clermont, Fairfield, etc.). Researchers must identify the correct county *at the time of the event*, not today. The rule: **records follow the jurisdiction that created them**, not modern county lines.
- **1803:** Ohio statehood. Remaining unorganized territory to the west and north became Indiana Territory.

### Geographic split (three land survey systems — search all three)
The Northwest Ordinance and subsequent acts created **three completely different land systems** within Ohio, each with its own survey method, record type, and repository. Which system applies depends on *where in Ohio* the ancestor lived:

| District | Location within Ohio | Survey system | Key repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers (south-central Ohio) | Metes-and-bounds (irregular) | Virginia State Library, Richmond |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio (roughly modern Lake, Geauga, Ashtabula, Trumbull, and adjacent counties) | Connecticut rectangular grid | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **US Congress Lands / Seven Ranges / BLM** | Remainder of Ohio (majority of the state) | Federal rectangular survey system | Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office (BLM GLO) website |

> **Critical quirk:** Unlike a simple before/after date rule, these three districts cover *different geographic zones*. Which repository holds an ancestor's land records depends entirely on where they lived within Ohio — not when. If you do not know the specific location, you may need to search all three repositories. Records that appear to be "missing" online are often simply held under a different system in a repository not digitized on FamilySearch.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records" and "Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes")*

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration of births and deaths in Ohio did **not** exist in 1790. Ohio's earliest county-level vital registration did not begin until well after statehood; statewide registration came even later.
- **What exists for 1790:** **Nothing by civil registration.** Church records are the only primary sources for births, baptisms, and deaths in this period.
- **Marriages:** County marriage registers began in some counties at or near their organization dates. FamilySearch holds **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (Collection ID 1803785; 1,523,678 records; 761,839 images). This collection's start date of 1789 aligns directly with Washington County's first year, making it the earliest civil vital record for the region. — **Indexed + images.**
- **Gaps:** No statewide coverage; coverage depends entirely on which county was operating and keeping records at the time. Washington County records from 1788–1790 are the earliest retrievable civil records.

### Church Records

- **Most important substitute source for 1790.** Baptisms, marriages, and burial records from early congregations predate civil registration by decades.
- FamilySearch holds **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (Collection ID 2246917; 678,234 records; 339,117 images). Starting date of 1787 directly covers the target period. — **Indexed + images** (verify coverage for specific county/denomination before assuming completeness).
- **Denominations with early Ohio presence:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker (Society of Friends). Quaker meeting records are particularly systematic and well-preserved; many are at the Ohio Yearly Meeting archives.
- **Physical repositories:** Denominational archives, local churches, and the Ohio History Connection hold records not fully digitized.

### Census Records

- **1790 Federal Census:** Ohio/Northwest Territory was **not enumerated** — it was not yet a state, and the 1790 federal census covered only the original thirteen states. This is the single largest documentation gap for the target period.
- **1800 Federal Census:** Ohio appeared for the first time, still as a territory. This is the earliest federal census covering the region and is a key surrogate for 1790 research — ancestors present in 1800 were likely there in 1790 as well.
- **1810 Federal Census:** First full enumeration after statehood (1803). Heads of household only (as with all censuses before 1850).
- **Territorial/state enumerations:** No territorial census is known to have been conducted for 1790 Ohio specifically.
- **Substitute:** Tax lists (below) function as a quasi-census for years without enumeration.

### Land Records — **The richest source for 1790**

Land records are the most abundant and genealogically informative source for this period. Three separate record systems apply:

**1. BLM General Land Office (Congress Lands / Seven Ranges)**
- Federal land patents are searchable free at the BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). The Seven Ranges (southeastern Ohio) were the first federal lands surveyed in the US, beginning 1786–1787.
- Records include original land patents naming the patentee, acreage, and legal description.

**2. Virginia Military District**
- Warrants (authorizations for land) issued to Virginia Revolutionary War veterans. Warrant records are at the **Virginia State Library and Archives**, Richmond.
- Survey plats and patents are also at the BLM GLO and at the Ohio History Connection.
- Many early settlers in south-central Ohio acquired land this way; if an ancestor was a Virginia veteran or purchased land from one, these warrant files may provide rich personal data.

**3. Connecticut Western Reserve**
- Land records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland.
- The Connecticut Land Company sold lots; company records identify purchasers.

**FamilySearch digitized collection:** **Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840** (Collection ID 1542187; 234,567 records; 117,283 images) — **Indexed + images.** Covers the target period from 1787.

**Volume on FamilySearch:** Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799 (Image Group 005112233; 51 images; **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable**) — **Browse-only.** Must be examined image by image with no search capability.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records")*

### Tax Records

- Washington County and Hamilton County began assessing taxes shortly after their organization (1788 and 1790, respectively).
- Tax lists name heads of household and taxable property and function as a census substitute for non-enumeration years.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (Collection ID 1987542; 345,890 records; 172,945 images) — **Indexed + images.** Note this collection begins at 1800, just after the target period; the 1790s records are the gap.
- **Volume on FamilySearch:** Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803 (Image Group 005112240; 73 images; **12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable**) — **Mostly browse-only**, with a small indexed fraction.
- For tax records predating 1799: physical or microfilm records at the Ohio History Connection and individual county courthouses.

### Probate and Court Records

- Washington County's General Court of Quarter Sessions began in 1788 and is the earliest court record for the Ohio region.
- Probate records include wills, estate inventories, guardianship appointments, and administration files — all rich for naming family members.
- **Where held:** Early court and land records (including probate) are at the **Ohio History Connection** (formerly Ohio Historical Society), 800 E. 17th Ave., Columbus — per the FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes."
- FamilySearch's digitized Ohio collections do not appear to include a standalone pre-statehood court/probate collection for this window in the tools searched; the Ohio History Connection is the authoritative physical repository.

### Military Records

- Revolutionary War veterans are heavily represented among early Ohio settlers — especially in the Virginia Military District. Pension files and bounty land warrant applications (at NARA) often contain biographical detail (birth place, age, family members, service history).
- Indian Wars (1790–1795): Service against the Western Confederacy (including the campaigns of Harmar, St. Clair, and Wayne) generated service records at NARA and at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Fold3** (subscription) holds digitized Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrants.
- **NARA** (archives.gov) holds original pension files, service records, and bounty land warrants.

### Church Records (expanded)

Already noted above; worth re-emphasizing: **for births and deaths in 1790, church registers are the only primary source.** Early Methodist circuit rider records, Presbyterian session minutes, Baptist church registers, and Quaker meeting minutes are the substitutes for absent civil registration.

### Cemetery Records

- Early grave markers often predate any other local record.
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) — free; extensive volunteer-transcribed coverage for Ohio.
- Physical cemetery records (sexton books) are at local churches or county historical societies.

### Newspapers

- No newspapers operated in the Northwest Territory before 1793. The first Ohio newspaper, the *Centinel of the North-Western Territory*, was founded in Cincinnati in 1793 — **after** the 1790 target date, though it becomes relevant for events in the immediately following years.
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) holds later Ohio newspapers. Not useful for 1790 itself.

### Immigration/Naturalization Records

- Naturalization was rare in the frontier period; formal naturalization courts barely existed in the territory.
- Most early Ohio settlers migrated overland from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and New England — not by international immigration — so passenger lists are not a primary tool here.
- For settlers who had immigrated from Europe in an earlier decade, check passenger list databases (NARA; Ancestry) for the port of arrival in the 1770s–1780s, not Ohio.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections / Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Ohio, County Marriages 1789–2013 (1.5M records); Ohio, Church Records 1787–1950 (678K records); Ohio, Land Records 1787–1840 (235K records); Ohio, Tax Records 1800–1850 (346K records); NW Territory Territorial Land Records 1788–1799 (browse-only, 51 images); Washington Co. Tax Records 1799–1803 (mostly browse-only, 73 images) | Free |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Congress Lands / Seven Ranges from 1787 onward; name-searchable | Free |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrants; Indian Wars service records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collection (1800, 1810 are first Ohio appearances); additional Ohio county records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Finding aids for pension files, land warrant files, territorial records | Free access to finding aids; some digital records |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus | Early territorial and county court records; land records; newspaper collection; state archives | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land company records; northeastern Ohio early records | In-person; some online |
| **Virginia State Library & Archives**, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrant files for pre-patent stage | In-person / correspondence |
| **County courthouses** (Washington, Hamilton, etc.) | Original deed books, probate files, marriage registers | In-person |
| **Denominational archives** | Church registers not yet digitized (Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker) | Varies by denomination |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Pre-1799 county tax lists** (Washington and Hamilton Counties, 1788–1799) — microfilm or physical at the Ohio History Connection; not digitized in indexed form on FamilySearch.
- **Early territorial court minutes** (Washington County General Court, 1788–1803) — largely physical at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Virginia Military District warrant files** at the Virginia State Library — not digitized on FamilySearch for this period.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve land company records** at the Western Reserve Historical Society — not digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Most church registers** for specific early congregations — especially Methodist circuit records and Baptist registers; microfilm at FHL in some cases but not in the indexed FamilySearch collections.

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **The 1790 federal census gap is the defining limitation:** the Northwest Territory was simply not enumerated. No territorial substitute enumeration is known.
- **County formation lag:** Before 1788 there is no formal county government at all. Even after Washington County's organization, record-keeping took time to become systematic on the frontier.
- **Early county court records:** Some early territorial court minutes are incomplete due to the frontier conditions of record-keeping; the Ohio History Connection can advise on specific survival status.
- **Indian Wars disruption:** Active conflict across most of the territory through 1795 disrupted settlement and record-creation in many areas.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the county, not the state.** In 1790, everything hinged on whether the ancestor was in Washington County (est. 1788) or Hamilton County (est. 1790). Identify the county first; it determines which court, tax list, and marriage register to search.

2. **Know your land district before searching land records.** If the ancestor lived between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers → Virginia Military District → Virginia State Library. Northeastern Ohio → Connecticut Western Reserve → Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland. Everywhere else → BLM GLO website. Searching the wrong system will produce false negatives.

3. **Use 1800 and 1810 censuses as proxies for 1790.** Ancestors present in 1800 were very likely in the territory in 1790. Work backward from 1800.

4. **Church records are the only birth/death source for 1790.** Do not assume a birth or burial was unrecorded — it may simply be in a church register rather than a civil registry. Check early Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker records for the relevant county.

5. **Look for Revolutionary War connections.** Many early Ohio settlers were veterans or their families. Pension files and bounty land warrant applications at NARA are genealogically rich and may be the best-documented source for an 1790-era ancestor.

6. **The FamilySearch NW Territory Territorial Land Records volume (Image Group 005112233) must be browsed image by image** — it is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable. Budget time for manual review of all 51 images if land records in the territorial period are relevant.

7. **Early county records may still be filed under the *parent* county name.** If Hamilton County was not yet organized at the time of an event, the record may be under Washington County — even for locations in southwestern Ohio. Check the county formation date against the event year.

---

*Sources: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory) and "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records); Wikipedia, "Ohio"; FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search results; external_links_search results for Ohio, United States, 1780–1810.*
