## 📋 Locality Research Guide
### Quaker Communities in Pennsylvania — Late 1700s (c. 1750–1800)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Standard place:** Pennsylvania, United States (state-level jurisdiction, founded 1682 by William Penn as an explicit Quaker haven).

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** until **1906** — meaning Quaker meeting records are not merely supplemental, they are the *primary* vital records source for births, marriages, and deaths in this period. This makes them exceptionally high-value for genealogical research.

The core Quaker counties in the late 1700s were **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware** counties, which held the densest meeting networks. Frontier counties (Lancaster, York, Berks) also had Quaker meetings but with thinner records survival.

---

### How Quaker Meetings Recorded Families

Understanding the meeting hierarchy is essential for knowing which records to seek:

| Level | Unit | What Was Recorded |
|---|---|---|
| **Monthly Meeting** | Core record-keeping unit | Births, marriages, deaths, disownments, certificates of removal |
| **Quarterly Meeting** | Regional grouping of monthly meetings | Business minutes; some oversight of monthly meeting affairs |
| **Yearly Meeting** | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (umbrella for most of PA) | Epistles, discipline, broad policy |

**Go to the monthly meeting first** — that is where individual family events appear. Quarterly and yearly meeting records are less genealogically granular.

---

### Record Types, Access & Repositories

#### 1. 🔑 Quaker Monthly Meeting Records *(primary source)*

The most important record class for this research. Monthly meetings documented:
- **Birth registers** — typically name, parents, date of birth
- **Marriage records** — Quaker marriages required no clergy; the meeting approved the union, the certificate was signed by *all attendees* (an extraordinary witness list), and the minute was recorded
- **Death registers** — name, date, sometimes burial location
- **Disownments** — members disciplined or expelled for violations (including military service during the Revolution — extremely common 1775–1783 and highly genealogically useful)
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when a member relocated to a new monthly meeting, documenting migration with family details

**Access:**
- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) — the single largest repository of American Quaker records; holds original registers and minutes for dozens of Pennsylvania monthly meetings. Access in person or via finding aids at [www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library).
- **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) — second major repository; strong holdings for Philadelphia-area meetings.
- **FamilySearch microfilm** — FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes and birth/death/marriage registers (per the FamilySearch Wiki article *Pennsylvania Church Records*).

**On FamilySearch — Digitized & Indexed:**
> **Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985** (Collection ID: 1401638)
> - 1,245,830 records | 982,415 persons | 607,220 images
> - Date range covers the full target period
> - **Access level: Indexed + images** — name-searchable
> - 🔗 [familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638)
> - *This is the key FamilySearch collection for Quaker meeting records in Pennsylvania.*

**On FamilySearch — Browse-only Volume:**
> **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** (Image Group: 001188322)
> - 145 images | **0% name-indexed | not full-text searchable**
> - ⚠️ **Browse-only** — must be examined image by image; no search capability
> - Yearly meeting minutes are less specific than monthly meeting records but document the institutional context

---

#### 2. 📖 Published Abstracts — Hinshaw's Encyclopedia

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** — abstracts birth, marriage, death, and removal entries from Pennsylvania meeting records into a searchable printed reference. This is often the fastest first-pass tool before going to original registers.

- Volumes covering Pennsylvania are widely held in genealogical libraries and are partially digitized on Archive.org and other platforms.
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki (*Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts*): Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia meetings are especially well represented.

---

#### 3. Probate Records

Wills and estate inventories name heirs, spouses, and sometimes grandchildren — essential for reconstructing family structure when meeting records are silent.

> **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (Collection ID: 1999196)
> - 893,214 records | 893,214 persons | 446,607 images
> - Covers 1750–1800 fully
> - **Access level: Indexed + images**
> - 🔗 [familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)

---

#### 4. Marriage Records (Civil & Compiled)

Two additional marriage collections overlap the target period and may include some Quaker unions entered into civil registers or compiled from other sources:

> **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (Collection ID: 1571957)
> - 312,045 records | 156,023 images
> - **Access level: Indexed + images**
> - 🔗 [familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)

> **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (Collection ID: 1502909)
> - 198,765 records | **no images** — index only
> - **Access level: Index only** — no original images available on FamilySearch
> - 🔗 [familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)

---

#### 5. Land Records & Tax Lists

Land ownership documents (deed books, warrants, surveys) are held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg). Tax lists from the 1760s–1790s often serve as a pre-census substitute and can place a family in a specific township — useful for identifying which monthly meeting had jurisdiction.

- **Pennsylvania State Archives** holds provincial and early state land records.
- **County deed books** are held at each county courthouse and many are microfilmed by FamilySearch.

---

#### 6. Federal Census — 1790

The first federal census (1790) covers Pennsylvania heads of household with household counts. It does not name women or children but confirms a family's presence in a specific county and township, allowing you to narrow the correct monthly meeting.
- Available indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

#### 7. Revolutionary War Records

Many Pennsylvania Quakers were **disowned by their monthly meetings** for participating in the Revolutionary War (a violation of the peace testimony). Disownment records in meeting minutes are a direct genealogical source. Conversely, those who *didn't* participate may appear in **conscientious objector** or substitute-fine records. Military pension files at NARA may also document Quaker family members.

---

### Key Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **No civil registration until 1906.** Meeting records *are* the vital records. If your ancestor was an active Friend, expect to find births, marriages, and deaths there — not in a courthouse.

2. **Start at the monthly meeting level, not the yearly meeting.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume on FamilySearch is browse-only and records institutional policy, not individual family events.

3. **Certificates of removal document migration.** When a Quaker family moved from one county (or state) to another, they requested a certificate of removal from their old meeting and presented it to the new one. Both meetings recorded the transaction — this is how you trace families across county or state lines.

4. **Disownment records are genealogically rich.** A disownment entry typically names the person, the offense, and often family relationships. Disownments for "marrying out of meeting" (wedding a non-Quaker) are especially common in this period.

5. **"Marrying out of meeting" creates a gap.** A Quaker who married a non-Friend was disowned, and the marriage would *not* appear in meeting records. Look to county civil records and supplementary collections in that case.

6. **Meeting boundaries ≠ county boundaries.** Identify the specific township where a family lived, then map it to the monthly meeting with geographic jurisdiction. The Friends Historical Library has meeting boundary maps.

7. **The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume is browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — plan time to review it image by image if needed.

8. **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The wiki place pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey — consult the specific FamilySearch Wiki article *[Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records)* directly for updated guidance.

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Original monthly meeting registers, minutes, and removal certificates for most PA meetings | In person; finding aids online |
| Haverford College Quaker Collections | Philadelphia-area meeting records; manuscripts | In person; some digitized |
| FamilySearch (Church & Town Records, 1708–1985) | Digitized & indexed PA church records incl. Quaker | Free online, name-searchable |
| FamilySearch (Philadelphia YM Minutes, 1750–1800) | 145-image browse-only volume | Free online, browse only |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants, provincial records, tax lists | In person; some microfilm |
| NARA (Philadelphia region) | Federal census (1790+), pension files, naturalizations | In person and online (Ancestry/Fold3) |
| Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* (print/digital) | Abstracts of PA meeting records | Libraries; Archive.org |

---

### Recommended Search Sequence

1. **Search FamilySearch Collection 1401638** (*Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985*) — the fastest indexed entry point for Quaker meeting data.
2. **Consult Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia*** for the relevant county to cross-check and fill gaps.
3. **Identify the correct monthly meeting** using the ancestor's township, then request original registers from **Friends Historical Library** or **Haverford College**.
4. **Track certificates of removal** to follow families across county or state lines.
5. **Cross-check with probate records** (Collection 1999196) and 1790 census to anchor the family in place and confirm household composition.
6. **For disowned ancestors**, search disownment minutes in the meeting records *and* in civil/county marriage records for "married out of meeting" unions.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (c. 1870–1905)
### Focus: Steel Industry Families & Occupational Sources

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **City / County** | Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania |
| **County formed** | 1788, from Westmoreland and Washington Counties |
| **Pittsburgh incorporated** | 1758 (settled); city charter 1816 |
| **County seat** | Pittsburgh |
| **Parent state** | Pennsylvania (one of the original 13 states) |
| **Population during period** | Pittsburgh grew explosively in this era driven by steel, coke, and glass manufacturing. Andrew Carnegie's steel empire and dozens of other industrial firms drew enormous immigrant labor streams from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, and Italy. |
| **Economy** | Steel production dominant; also iron, coke, glass, aluminum, and river trade. The Homestead Strike of 1892 is a major landmark event for this period. |
| **Religious denominations** | Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, German Lutheran, Serbian and Russian Orthodox, Jewish |
| **Key events** | Homestead Strike (1892); Great Railroad Strike (1877); massive immigration wave (1880s–1900s) |

---

## Boundary Changes

Allegheny County boundaries were **stable throughout the late 1800s** — no splits or mergers affected it during this period. Pittsburgh itself annexed neighboring boroughs and townships during this era (notably annexing Allegheny City in 1907, just after the period). Records for mill towns immediately surrounding Pittsburgh (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne) were created at the **township or borough level**, not the city of Pittsburgh, and are held under those sub-jurisdictions at the county level.

> **Quirk:** Mill workers living in Homestead, Braddock, or McKeesport are NOT in Pittsburgh city records — search at the township/borough level within Allegheny County.

---

## Available Record Types

### ⚙️ Industrial & Occupational Records *(the core of your research)*

This is the most distinctive and valuable record category for Pittsburgh steel-era research — and the most fragmented.

| Source | What it contains | Where held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Payroll, hire/termination dates, job classification, sometimes birthplace and next of kin | **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** | Physical only — fragmentary survival; contact archives for specific firms |
| **Carnegie Steel / U.S. Steel records** | Partial personnel files; some payroll ledgers survive | Heinz History Center; some at **Hagley Museum & Library** (Wilmington, DE) | Physical only |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Lists mills inspected, worker counts, accident reports; names appear when accidents are documented | **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Physical only; some published reports may be online |
| **Union membership lists** | Names, dues records, sometimes home addresses | **Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers** records — partially at Heinz History Center; **United Steelworkers archives** (Pittsburgh) | Physical only — contact archives directly |
| **City directories** | Occupation, employer, home address; annual volumes from 1813 onward | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (complete run from 1810s); some volumes digitized on **Ancestry.com** and **FamilySearch** | Physical at Carnegie Library; partial indexed access online |
| **Federal census occupation columns** | 1870, 1880, 1900 census all record occupation — iron/steel worker entries allow reconstruction of workforce | FamilySearch, Ancestry (indexed + images) | **Indexed + images online** |

> **Strategy tip:** City directories are your best annual locator between census years. They list occupation and employer, which lets you track a worker's movements between mills from year to year. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds the most complete run in the region.

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Critical gap:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. For the late 1800s, Allegheny County recorded births and deaths locally beginning around **1870**, but coverage is incomplete and inconsistent before statewide law took effect.
- **What to expect:** County birth and death registers (1870–1905) exist for Allegheny County but are not comprehensively indexed online. Church records are often the **better source** for vital events in this period.
- **Marriages:** Kept at the county level from the colonial period. FamilySearch has:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — **524,189 records / 312,045 images** — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — **312,045 records / 156,023 images** — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — **198,765 records / no images** — **index only, no images**
- **Death certificates (statewide):** Begin **1906** — just after the core period but valuable for workers who died from industrial injury or disease in the early 1900s. FamilySearch: *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* — **4,218,763 records / images — indexed + images**

---

### Church Records

Church registers are **the primary vital records source** for this period — more reliable than the patchy pre-1906 county registration.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* — **1,245,830 records / 607,220 images** — mix of indexed and browse-only depending on the specific congregation
- **Ethnic Catholic parishes** (the most genealogically rich for immigrant mill workers):
  - Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian parishes each maintained separate registers — baptisms, confirmations, marriages, and burials — in their heritage language
  - These registers are **the best source** for family relationships, godparents (often relatives), and original village names in the Old Country
  - Diocesan archives: **Diocese of Pittsburgh** holds many original registers; others remain at individual parishes
- **Protestant:** Presbyterian and Methodist registers; German Lutheran parishes maintain records in German through the early 1880s
- **Eastern Orthodox:** Serbian and Russian Orthodox communities formed parishes from the 1890s onward

> **Quirk:** Catholic parish registers for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers are often in Latin (sacramental entries) with names and marginalia in the heritage language. Reading them requires knowledge of both Latin formularies and the vernacular.

---

### Census Records

| Census Year | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1870** | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Lists occupation — identify steelworkers |
| **1880** | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Most complete for mid-period; Soundex index |
| **1890** | Largely destroyed (fire, 1921) | Veterans' schedule partially survives — check for Civil War veterans in the household |
| **1900** | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Lists years in the US, citizenship status — critical for immigrant workers |
| **1880 Mortality Schedule** | Browse-only on FamilySearch | Records deaths in the year preceding the census — captures industrial accident victims |

> **Strategy:** Run the 1880 and 1900 census for every known family member. The 1900 schedule's "years in US" and "number of children born / living" columns are particularly valuable for immigrant families.

---

### Naturalization Records

A **top-priority record class** for immigrant steel workers — it often gives the exact village of origin in the home country.

- **Pre-1906:** Any court of record could naturalize — in Allegheny County this means the **Court of Common Pleas**, the **District Court**, and the **Orphans' Court** all issued papers. Declarations and petitions are at the **Allegheny County Courthouse** (some microfilmed by FamilySearch).
- **Post-1906:** Centralized through the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization — records at **National Archives at Philadelphia** (Mid-Atlantic Region).
- **Access:** Partially microfilmed; some indexed on **Ancestry** (Pennsylvania Naturalization Records collections). The original papers — especially the petition — list birthplace, arrival date, physical description, and witnesses (often relatives or coworkers).

---

### Immigration Records (Passenger Lists)

Pittsburgh's immigrant workforce arrived primarily through **Philadelphia** and **Baltimore** (before 1890) and then increasingly through **New York / Castle Garden / Ellis Island** (from 1892). Key collections:

- **Passenger lists (all ports):** Indexed + images on **Ancestry** and **FamilySearch**. From 1895 onward, manifests list hometown and nearest relative in the home country.
- **Baltimore steamship manifests** (1820–1891): Significant for German, Irish, and some Slavic immigrants
- **Ellis Island arrivals** (1892–1957): Indexed at **libertyellisfoundation.org** and **Ancestry**

> **Note:** Passenger lists from 1895 onward record the immigrant's contact person in the US — often an already-settled relative — as well as who they were traveling to. This can reveal family clusters in Pittsburgh mill neighborhoods.

---

### Probate Records

- FamilySearch: *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* — **893,214 records / 446,607 images — indexed + images**
- Originals held at **Allegheny County Register of Wills** (Pittsburgh)
- Estate inventories list household goods and debts — useful for establishing economic status; workers killed in industrial accidents may have intestate proceedings

---

### Land Records

- Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** (not federal land) — original grants from William Penn's Land Office
- **Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds** holds deed books from 1788
- Workers in rented mill housing may appear in **landlord deed records** and **tax assessment rolls** rather than deed transfers
- Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds the original Land Office warrants and surveys

---

### Military Records

- Many late-1800s Pittsburgh steelworkers were **Civil War veterans** — pension files at NARA often provide detailed biographical information (birthplace, marriage date, children)
- **1890 Veterans' Schedule** (the one surviving fragment of the 1890 census): Check this for Allegheny County veterans
- Spanish-American War (1898): Service records at NARA; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records
- **Fold3.com:** Indexed access to Civil War pension files and service records

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Allegheny Cemetery** (Pittsburgh) — large non-sectarian cemetery; sexton records survive
- **St. Mary's Cemetery**, **Calvary Catholic Cemetery**, **Homewood Cemetery**: Major Catholic cemeteries with ethnic sections
- **FindAGrave.com**: Significant coverage for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries; many headstones photographed
- Sexton records (burial registers) for some cemeteries are held at the **Heinz History Center**

---

### Newspaper Records

| Paper | Date range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pittsburgh Gazette / Pittsburgh Post-Gazette | 1786–present | Obituaries, accident reports, strike coverage |
| Pittsburgh Press | 1884–1992 | Labor news, ethnic community columns |
| Pittsburgh Catholic | 1844–present | Catholic community news, death notices |
| Ethnic press (Polish, Slovak, German, Italian) | Various 1880s–1900s | Vital notices, community events in heritage language |

- **Newspapers.com** and **GenealogyBank**: Subscriptions; digitized Pittsburgh-area papers
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**: Microfilm holdings; some digital access
- Industrial accidents and labor disputes were **front-page news** — a worker killed at a mill will often appear in the Pittsburgh Gazette with name, neighborhood, and family details

---

### Tax Records

- Allegheny County tax assessment records from 1788 — useful as annual census substitutes and to track property ownership
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** holds some assessment duplicates
- Workers in company-owned mill housing may not appear as property owners, but **personal property tax lists** can still place them in a ward or township

---

### Fraternal, Mutual Aid & Ethnic Organization Records

An underused but extremely rich record class for immigrant workers:

| Organization type | Records created | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| Slovak, Polish, Croatian mutual aid societies | Membership rolls, death benefits, often birthplace and next of kin | Ethnic organizational archives; some at Heinz History Center |
| Knights of Labor / AFL unions | Membership cards, meeting minutes | Heinz History Center; United Steelworkers archives |
| Fraternal orders (Masons, Odd Fellows, etc.) | Membership records with biographical data | Grand Lodge archives; local lodge records |

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key collections for Pittsburgh 1870–1905 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church & Town Records 1708–1985; County Marriages 1885–1950; Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; Probate Records 1683–1994; Death Certificates 1906–1968; Federal census 1870–1900 | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census 1870–1900; Pennsylvania naturalization records; Pittsburgh city directories; passenger lists (all ports); Death certificates; some church records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank** | Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Press, Pittsburgh Catholic | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records, headstone photos | Free |
| **Fold3** | Military pension files, Civil War service records | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Passenger lists, post-1906 naturalization, federal court records | Free (in person) / some online via Ancestry |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Industrial company records; union archives; immigration records; Western Pennsylvania Genealogical Society collection; city directories; photographs | In-person; some by appointment |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** (Homestead, PA) | Mill-specific records, oral histories, photographs of Homestead / Braddock / Duquesne mills | Contact archives; some records fragmentary |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories from 1810s; local history collection; newspaper microfilm; Pittsburgh Catholic microfilm | In-person; some digital access |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage records; naturalization records (pre-1906); probate records; deed books | In-person / mail requests |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Land Office records; factory inspector reports; state census; military records | In-person; some records on microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** (Mid-Atlantic Region) | Post-1906 naturalization records; federal census; passenger lists (some); federal court records | In-person; appointments recommended |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers; confirmation records | Contact for access |
| **Hagley Museum & Library** (Wilmington, DE) | Carnegie Steel and U.S. Steel corporate records | In-person; research appointments |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following records exist but are **not available in any online database** and require contacting the holding repository directly:

- **Company employment / payroll records** (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, Westinghouse) — fragmentary survivors at Heinz History Center and Hagley
- **Union membership lists** (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers; early AFL affiliates)
- **State factory inspector reports** naming accident victims
- **Ethnic mutual aid society membership rolls** (Polish, Slovak, Croatian fraternal organizations)
- **Pre-1906 Allegheny County birth and death registers** — partially microfilmed but not fully indexed online
- **Sexton / burial registers** for most Pittsburgh Catholic cemeteries

---

## Known Record Losses & Gaps

| Loss | Impact | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|
| **1890 Federal Census** (fire, 1921) | A full decade of household data lost | 1890 Veterans' Schedule (partial); city directories 1889–1891; tax records |
| **Pre-1906 statewide vital registration** | Births and deaths not systematically recorded before 1906 | Church registers; county-level Allegheny County records (from ~1870); newspaper notices |
| **Industrial company records** | Most large steel firms did not preserve employee records systematically; fires and corporate mergers destroyed much | City directories; census occupation columns; union records; newspaper accident reports |

---

## Research Tips & Recommended Sequence

1. **Start with federal census** (1880 and 1900) to locate the family in a specific ward and identify occupations. The 1900 schedule's immigration data is especially valuable.

2. **Mine city directories annually** between census years. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh directories from the 1810s; Ancestry has digitized many volumes. They track household moves, job changes, and can establish exact death windows (name drops off the directory).

3. **Identify the ethnic parish.** For Catholic immigrant workers, the parish register is the most information-rich vital record source. Determine which ethnic parish served the neighborhood (e.g., Polish workers in Lawrenceville attended different parishes than Slovak workers in Homestead). Contact the **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** or the surviving parish directly.

4. **Search naturalization records early.** The petition for naturalization (post-1906) routinely gives birthplace, arrival date, and witnesses. Pre-1906 declarations at the Allegheny County courthouse are the equivalent.

5. **Check passenger lists for whole families.** All passengers aboard are listed — including infants and children traveling with parents. The contact person already in Pittsburgh is often a relative who can open a new research branch.

6. **Contact the Heinz History Center** before assuming company records don't exist. Their Western Pennsylvania Genealogical Society collection and industrial archives are the single richest physical repository for this subject and are not comprehensively described online.

7. **Search ethnic newspapers.** Slovak, Polish, and Croatian papers ran death notices, birth announcements, and community news that do not appear in English-language papers. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm runs of several ethnic papers.

8. **Use obituaries aggressively.** Even one-paragraph Pittsburgh Gazette obituaries for a mill worker in the 1880s–1900s often give birthplace, surviving children's names and addresses, lodge membership, and cause of death.

9. **Note the 1892 Homestead Strike.** Workers who participated were blacklisted and documented in both company records and press coverage. If your ancestor worked at Homestead Steel before and after 1892, the gap in records may reflect the strike's aftermath.

---

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Place:** Philadelphia County (County) and Philadelphia City (City), Pennsylvania, United States. Both have been separate but co-extensive jurisdictions since 1682. In 1793, the city of Philadelphia was one municipality within the larger county; other municipalities (Southwark, Northern Liberties) also fell within the county bounds. The city and county were formally consolidated only in 1854 — for 1793 research, be alert to which municipality within the county your family lived in.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (also the U.S. national capital in 1793)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population:** Approximately 50,000 in the city in 1793, per Wikipedia's article on the epidemic. No place-population data was returned by the FamilySearch tool for this jurisdiction and period.
- **Key historical event:** The yellow fever epidemic of 1793 struck August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the city's population (Wikipedia, *Yellow fever epidemic of 1793*). Thousands more fled to the countryside, creating sudden gaps in Philadelphia records and corresponding traces in suburban and rural Pennsylvania records.

---

## Boundary Notes

- Philadelphia County dates to 1682 and its boundaries were stable through the epidemic period.
- **The 1854 Act of Consolidation** merged the city and county, but this is irrelevant to 1793 — pre-1854 records may be filed under the specific municipality (Philadelphia City, Southwark, Northern Liberties, etc.), not merely "Philadelphia County." Knowing which ward or district your ancestor lived in is important for locating records.
- No mid-period boundary changes affect the 1780–1810 research window.

---

## Available Record Types

### ⚠️ Critical Baseline: No Civil Vital Registration in 1793

Pennsylvania did **not** have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. The earliest FamilySearch collection for Pennsylvania death certificates ("Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968," collection 2255317) begins in **1906** — 113 years after the epidemic. There are **no government-issued death certificates for 1793 victims**. Church records and epidemic-specific sources (below) are the primary substitutes.

---

### 1. Epidemic-Specific Sources ⭐ (Unique to 1793)

These sources are directly tied to the yellow fever outbreak and have no equivalent for other periods. They are your first stop.

| Source | What it Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey's published account** (*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever*, 1793) | Lists names of the dead; contemporaneous eyewitness account | Historical Society of Pennsylvania; published and digitized — searchable online |
| **Minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens** | Official relief committee records documenting deaths, aid distribution, and survivor petitions | Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania |
| **Bush Hill hospital records** | Records of the emergency fever hospital established during the epidemic | Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania |

> Per the FamilySearch Wiki's *Philadelphia Genealogy* article (section "Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793"): "Key genealogical sources include: burial records from Christ Church, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), and other churches; the published account by Mathew Carey listing names of the dead; minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens; and the records of Bush Hill hospital. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives hold manuscript sources."

Access: **Physical only** for manuscript Committee and Bush Hill records (HSP and Philadelphia City Archives); Carey's printed account has been digitized and is findable online through archive.org and Google Books.

---

### 2. Church Records ⭐ (Primary Source for 1793 Vital Events)

Because there was no civil registration, **church burial registers are the principal death records for the epidemic**. Philadelphia's religiously diverse community means records are scattered across many denominations.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* (collection ID 1401638) — 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images. This collection spans the 1793 period and includes Philadelphia church records. **Digitization level: indexed + images** (name-searchable on FamilySearch).
- **Named churches with 1793 burial records** (per FamilySearch Wiki *Philadelphia Genealogy*):
  - **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — one of the most prominent epidemic burial registers
  - **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' Church** (Swedish Lutheran, later Episcopal) — another named source for 1793 burials
  - Additional denominations present in 1793 Philadelphia included: Society of Friends (Quakers), First Presbyterian, German Reformed, German Lutheran, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Methodist Episcopal, and Baptist congregations — each kept their own registers.
- **Published transcriptions:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki, "many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published." The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (GSP) has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records.
- **Language note:** German Reformed and German Lutheran registers may be in German; Swedish records at Gloria Dei may be in Swedish for the earliest entries.
- **Where held:** Parish offices, Philadelphia Archdiocesan/diocesan archives, FamilySearch microfilm, GSP, and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Many are also in FamilySearch collection 1401638.

---

### 3. Census Records

| Census | Year | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1790 Federal Census | 1790 | 3 years *before* the epidemic — establishes households in Philadelphia before outbreak. Names heads of household only; other members counted by age/sex category only. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry, indexed. |
| 1800 Federal Census | 1800 | 7 years *after* — documents survivor households; useful for identifying families who fled and didn't return, or who lost members. Indexed + images. |

There was **no Pennsylvania state census** for this period. The federal censuses are the bracketing enumerations. Comparing 1790 and 1800 household composition can reveal epidemic losses or flight.

---

### 4. Probate Records

The surge of deaths in August–November 1793 produced a corresponding surge in probate filings. Philadelphia County probate records are a key source for identifying survivors, heirs, and family relationships after epidemic deaths.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection ID 1999196) — 893,214 records, 446,607 images. Covers 1793. **Digitization level: indexed + images.**
- Wills and letters of administration filed in late 1793 and 1794 should be searched for any ancestor believed to have died in the epidemic.
- Where held physically: Register of Wills, Philadelphia County; also at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 5. Vital Records — Marriage

Civil death registration didn't exist, but some civil marriage records predate statewide registration.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection ID 1571957) — 312,045 records, 156,023 images. Covers the 1793 period. **Digitization level: indexed + images.**
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection ID 1502909) — 198,765 records, **no images** (index only). Check for names but be aware there is no underlying image to view. **Digitization level: index only.**
- Church marriage registers (in collection 1401638, above) are often richer than civil records for this period.

---

### 6. Land and Tax Records

Families who fled Philadelphia during the epidemic may appear in land and tax records in surrounding counties. Within Philadelphia:

- **Deed books:** Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds. Deeds record property sales that may follow epidemic deaths (estates selling property, heirs dividing land). Not reported as a digitized FamilySearch collection in the 1750–1820 search window.
- **Tax lists:** Philadelphia assessment lists and tax records survive from the late 18th century. These can substitute for census data and confirm residence. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP; some are published or microfilmed.
- **Pennsylvania land records** use a metes-and-bounds system (Pennsylvania is a state-land state); the Pennsylvania State Archives holds original land grants and warrants.

---

### 7. Court Records

- Philadelphia's Court of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and Orphans' Court records survive from the colonial period. Orphans' Court records (guardianships of orphaned children) would be particularly relevant if a parent died in the epidemic.
- Held at the Philadelphia City Archives; some on microfilm at the Family History Library.

---

### 8. Newspaper Records

Philadelphia newspapers in 1793 published extensive lists of the dead, notices of estates, and accounts of families who fled.

- Key papers of the period: *General Advertiser*, *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *Pennsylvania Packet*, *Federal Gazette*.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) cover some Philadelphia papers; historical library collections (HSP, Library Company of Philadelphia) hold physical runs. Curated external links for this place/period from FamilySearch's directory pointed to Newspapers.com (generic link).
- Death notices and estate notices published in August–November 1793 can document epidemic victims not found in church registers.

---

### 9. Military Records

The epidemic period overlaps with early U.S. military service. Philadelphia men who served in the Revolutionary War or the 1790s militia may have pension files.

- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Fold3 (subscription) curates military records including pension files.
- Revolutionary War pension files (NARA M804) are indexed and searchable on Fold3 and FamilySearch; they name spouses and children and can establish family structure around 1793.

---

### 10. Immigration Records

Philadelphia was the leading port of entry in the late 18th century. Many Philadelphia families in 1793 were first- or second-generation immigrants.

- Passenger arrival lists for Philadelphia survive from the 1700s and are held at NARA and the Philadelphia City Archives.
- Naturalization records (pre-1906) were filed at multiple courts — Philadelphia Common Pleas, District Court, and others.
- NARA is the primary repository; some records are on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's list.** His 1793 published account includes names of the dead and is freely available digitized online — it is your fastest first check for an ancestor who may have died in the epidemic.

2. **No death certificate exists for 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906. Do not search for one. Go directly to church burial registers and the Carey list.

3. **Search the bracketing censuses together.** Compare 1790 and 1800 federal census households for your Philadelphia family. Disappearances between the two enumerations, or household composition changes, can indicate epidemic deaths.

4. **Check probate records immediately after a suspected death.** The surge of 1793–1794 Philadelphia probate filings is well-documented. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (*Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994*) is indexed and searchable — run your surname against it for 1793–1796.

5. **Identify your ancestor's denomination.** Philadelphia's many denominations kept separate registers. Knowing whether your family was Quaker, Anglican, Lutheran, Catholic, or Presbyterian focuses the church record search considerably. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled indexes can help you narrow denomination.

6. **Search surrounding counties for refugees.** Thousands fled Philadelphia in August 1793. Chester, Montgomery, Bucks, and Delaware county records (church registers, tax lists, tavern licenses) may document your ancestor's temporary or permanent relocation.

7. **Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania** (the city) and **Philadelphia, Pennsylvania** (the county) are two distinct FamilySearch jurisdictions — search both when using place-based filters, as records may be filed under either.

8. **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has published and indexed many church records not otherwise findable online. Their *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* and other publications are worth checking for your surname and church.

9. **Newspapers are an underused source.** Death notices, estate notices, and lists of epidemic dead appeared in Philadelphia papers from August–November 1793. The Library Company of Philadelphia and HSP hold runs of period papers.

10. **Consider DNA evidence** as a supplement where documentary records are sparse — particularly useful if an ancestor fled and lost touch with their Philadelphia origin community.

## 📋 Locality Research Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Fire Era, c. 1840–1900

> **Standard place:** Chicago, Cook, Illinois, United States
> **Focus:** Records for families affected by the Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871

---

### ⚠️ The Fire and Its Impact on Records — Read This First

The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, which housed virtually all of the city's official pre-1871 records: deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls. This is the single most defining fact of Cook County genealogical research. Almost no civil records survive from before October 10, 1871.

**The critical rule:** treat pre- and post-fire research as two distinct phases with different source strategies.

---

### Phase 1: Pre-Fire Chicago (before October 10, 1871)

Because virtually all local civil records were lost, you must rely entirely on **substitute sources**. The following survived:

#### 🗳️ Federal Census Records — **★ Most Important Pre-Fire Substitute**
- The **1870 federal census** is the single best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families. It survived because the original schedules were held in **Washington, D.C.**, not in Chicago. This is indexed and available on [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- Earlier censuses: **1840, 1850, 1860** also survive and are indexed.
- ⚠️ The **1890 federal census** was largely destroyed in a separate Washington fire (1921) — a gap affecting the immediate post-fire generation.

#### 📒 City Directories — **Essential Substitute**
- Chicago city directories were published **from 1839 onward** and many survive. They list heads of household by name, occupation, and address — functioning as an annual "census."
- **Held at:** The **Newberry Library** (Chicago), which has the most complete run. Some years are digitized on Ancestry.com and on HathiTrust.
- Use these to establish residence in Chicago before the fire and to track family mobility year by year.

#### ⛪ Church Records — **Primary Vital Record Substitute**
- Many church registers **survived** because they were held at parish buildings outside the fire zone, or were re-established from memory and surviving copies shortly after.
- FamilySearch holds **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** — approximately 285,000 records, covering Catholic, Lutheran, Episcopal, and other denominations. This collection spans the fire and is a primary resource.
- **Catholic parishes:** The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds original registers. Many immigrant communities (German, Polish, Irish, Bohemian) maintained their own parish records independently of civil registration.
- If a specific parish's records are missing, check whether a neighboring parish of the same denomination absorbed its congregation after the fire.

#### 📜 Naturalization Records — **Key for Immigrant Families**
- Cook County **Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s** — they were not all housed in the courthouse building that burned.
- These records can establish immigration date, country of origin, and sometimes names of family members.
- **Held at:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University; also microfilmed by FamilySearch.

#### 🏠 Land and Property — Pre-Fire
- Virtually all pre-fire deeds are gone. However, **insurance company records**, particularly the **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection**, became vital substitutes for pre-fire property ownership.
- **Held at:** The **Chicago History Museum**, which holds this collection along with photographs and personal papers from the fire era.

---

### Phase 2: Post-Fire Reconstruction (1871 and after)

#### 📄 The Burnt Record Act (1872) — Property Re-Recordings
- Illinois passed the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, requiring property owners to re-register their deeds. This created a new set of property records and is a critical source for establishing who owned land in Chicago before the fire.
- FamilySearch has digitized post-fire property re-recordings (**imageGroupNumber 009982111**, 112 images, 1871–1880): approximately **41% is name-indexed** (searchable by name), the remainder must be browsed image by image. Not full-text searchable.

#### 📋 Civil Vital Records — Post-Fire Originals
Cook County began systematic registration after the fire. All three collections are on FamilySearch:

| Collection | Date Range | Record Count | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Birth Certificates** | 1871–1940 | ~1,450,000 | Indexed + images |
| **Death Records** | 1871–1947 | ~980,000 | Indexed + images |
| **Marriage Records** | 1871–1920 | ~620,000 | Indexed + images |

> ⚠️ Note: **Illinois statewide** vital registration did not begin until 1916. These Cook County records are locally created — don't assume statewide coverage. For births and deaths outside Cook County before 1916, substitute sources are required.

#### 📑 Reconstructed Pre-Fire Court Records
FamilySearch holds a browse-only volume of **reconstructed Cook County court records, 1865–1871** (imageGroupNumber 009982110, 38 images). These are copies assembled after the fire. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.**

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories (1839+), maps, manuscripts, genealogy reference collection | In-person; some materials digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, photographs, personal papers, fire-era documents | In-person research; finding aids online |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward (originals) | In-person or written request |
| **IRAD – Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County records post-1871; naturalization records; court files | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago – Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | In-person by appointment |
| **Illinois State Archives (Springfield)** | Military records, state census fragments, land patent records | In-person and online partial indexes |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal census, passenger lists, military service records, pension files | Online via Ancestry, Fold3, FamilySearch |

---

### Other Record Types to Search

#### 🪖 Military Records
- Civil War service and pension files at **NARA** (via [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry.com). Men who served in Illinois units can be traced through the **Illinois Adjutant General's records** at the Illinois State Archives.
- Draft registration records (Civil War era) survive independently of the courthouse.

#### 📰 Newspapers
- Chicago newspapers (**Chicago Tribune**, **Chicago Times**, others) survived the fire and extensively covered the disaster — including lists of the dead, homeless, and those seeking missing relatives. Post-fire editions are a rich but underused source.
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) and the **Newberry Library** hold the best runs.
- The Chicago Tribune's October–November 1871 issues are particularly valuable for fire victim and survivor identification.

#### ⚰️ Cemetery Records
- Many Chicago-area cemeteries (Graceland, Rosehill, St. Boniface, Mount Olivet) predate the fire and their sexton's records survive.
- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) and [BillionGraves](https://billiongraves.com/) have indexed many headstones.
- Physical burial registers are held at the individual cemetery offices.

#### 🚢 Immigration & Passenger Lists
- NARA holds passenger arrival lists. Pre-1891 arrivals entered via New York and other Atlantic ports; lists are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- For German, Scandinavian, Irish, and Bohemian immigrants who settled in Chicago, Hamburg emigration lists and home-country records may fill gaps.

#### 📐 Land & Probate (Post-Fire)
- Probate records from 1871 onward are at the **Cook County Probate Court** and at IRAD.
- Pre-fire probate is largely lost; check for any copies or references in newspaper legal notices or insurance records.

---

### Digitization Gaps to Be Aware Of

- **Pre-1871 civil records** are almost entirely destroyed — no digitization can restore what burned.
- **Pre-fire church records** that survived are partially microfilmed, but many denominational archives have not been fully digitized; in-person visits may be necessary.
- **1890 federal census** is destroyed for the entire U.S. — use state census substitutes (Illinois has none for this period) or city directories to bridge 1880–1900.
- The **Newberry Library's city directory collection** is largely physical-only for the earliest years.

---

### Research Strategy Summary for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it's the closest surviving snapshot before the fire.
2. **Search city directories 1860–1880** to track family location and occupation across the fire.
3. **Check church records** (FamilySearch collection 1803978) — the most likely source of pre-fire vital events.
4. **Search naturalization records** at IRAD if the family was immigrant (very likely in 1870s Chicago).
5. **Use post-fire vital records** (birth, death, marriage) for any events after October 1871.
6. **Search Chicago Tribune October–November 1871** for fire-era lists of victims, survivors, and the displaced.
7. **Contact the Chicago History Museum** for insurance and property records as a deed substitute.
8. **Check Burnt Record Act re-recordings** on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111) for post-fire property registration.

## Locality Research Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (c. 1699–1769)

### Jurisdictional Context

**French Louisiana (La Louisiane)** was an administrative district of New France. France controlled the territory from 1682 until the **Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)**, which ceded the lands west of the Mississippi to Spain. Spain assumed active administrative control around **1769**, ending the French colonial era for genealogical purposes. New Orleans was founded in 1718, which is the effective start date for most surviving records. Events before 1718 have extremely sparse documentation.

The colony was governed by the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**, not by counties — Louisiana used **administrative districts and posts**, not parishes (the parish/county structure came later). There was **no civil registration system**; the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under the Code Noir. All French colonial records are in **French**.

> ⚠️ **Critical transition quirk:** In 1762/1769 administration shifted to Spain. Spanish-era records (1769–1803) are in Spanish and filed under a different administrative structure. If your ancestor bridges this period, you must work both French and Spanish record sets.

---

### Record Types, Access, and Repositories

#### 1. 🏛 Catholic Parish Registers — **PRIME SOURCE**
*Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers)*

- **Why they matter:** The Catholic Church was the *only* legally recognized church in French Louisiana. Parish registers are the principal substitute for civil registration and the main source of vital family data.
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans:** Registers survive from **1720**. The Code Noir also mandated baptism of all enslaved persons, so these registers document both free and enslaved individuals.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — ~987,654 records with ~493,827 images. The date range **begins 1718**, making this the primary FamilySearch entry point for the French colonial period. Access level: **indexed + images**.
- **Language:** All entries are in French. You must be able to read French script of the period (or use a translator).
- **Repository:** Originals held at St. Louis Cathedral Archives and the Louisiana Historical Center; FamilySearch has digitized significant portions.

#### 2. 📜 Superior Council Records
*Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories*

- The Superior Council was the colony's governing and judicial body. Its records cover legal disputes, property, contracts, and inventories — highly genealogically useful when parish registers are silent.
- **Repository:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans. Partially digitized per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records").
- **Access level:** Partially digitized; physical access required for undigitized portions. Records are in French.

#### 3. 📑 Notarial Records
*Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions*

- The New Orleans Notarial Archives is the **oldest continuous notarial office in North America**, with records surviving from the **1730s** onward (per the FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants").
- These records are particularly valuable for marriage contracts, property transactions, and wills not captured in probate files.
- **Repository:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — provides public access.
- **Access level:** Some digitized; physical access available at the Research Center. Records in French.

#### 4. ⚖️ Probate Records
*Estate inventories, wills, administration*

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images. Date range begins **1756**, covering the final decade of the French colonial period. Access level: **indexed + images**.
- Colonial-era entries will be in French and follow French legal traditions.

#### 5. 🌍 French National Archives (ANOM) — *France-held records*
*Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls*

- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and **census rolls (recensements)** for the colony of Louisiana — records that were never transferred to Louisiana and are not in U.S. repositories.
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki, this is the repository for colonial-era administrative and population records.
- **Access:** Some ANOM records are available online at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr); physical access available in Aix-en-Provence.
- This repository is **essential** for tracing colonial settlers, military personnel, and administrators not well-documented in local Louisiana records.

#### 6. 🗺 Land Grants (Concessions)
*Colonial land records*

- French land concessions followed French legal traditions — not English common law. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, they are documented in:
  - **American State Papers: Public Lands** series
  - **Louisiana State Land Office** records
- These grants name grantees and sometimes family relationships.

---

### External Links & Third-Party Repositories

The FamilySearch curated link set for Louisiana returns 6 total resources, but for the 1700–1769 window the matches are **general repositories** (NARA, Ancestry census collections, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) rather than specialized French-colonial databases. For this period, the specialized repositories named above (ANOM, Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans Notarial Archives) are more directly relevant than the standard aggregator sites.

---

### Record Coverage & Gaps

| Record Type | Earliest Date | FamilySearch Access | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catholic parish registers | 1718 (St. Louis Cathedral) | Indexed + images (Coll. 1612905) | French |
| Probate records | 1756 | Indexed + images (Coll. 2078341) | French |
| Superior Council records | ~1712 | Partially digitized | French |
| Notarial records | 1730s | Some digitized; physical access | French |
| ANOM census & admin records | 1699+ | Some online (anom.fr) | French |
| Events before 1718 | pre-1718 | ⚠️ Extremely sparse | French |

---

### Key Quirks for This Period

1. **No civil registration.** There was no government vital records system in French Louisiana. Catholic sacramental registers *are* the vital records. If a baptism, marriage, or burial wasn't recorded by a priest, it almost certainly wasn't recorded at all.
2. **All records are in French.** Competence in 18th-century French (including Latin in church entries) is required. Consider engaging a professional translator for handwritten colonial documents.
3. **Code Noir and enslaved ancestors.** The Code Noir legally required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved people. Sacramental registers therefore contain entries for enslaved individuals — often by first name only with the enslaver named. This is a primary avenue for tracing enslaved ancestors in this period.
4. **No county/parish structure yet.** The modern Louisiana parish (county equivalent) system did not exist. Records were generated at administrative posts and the colonial capital (New Orleans). Do not search by modern parish name for French colonial events.
5. **ANOM is irreplaceable.** Many colonial-era census rolls and administrative records were sent to France and remain there. Domestic U.S. repositories alone are insufficient for a thorough French colonial search.
6. **The transition to Spain (1769).** If your ancestor appears in both French and Spanish-era records, be aware the two administrative regimes produced very different record types in different languages. Search both independently.
7. **Records before 1720 are extremely sparse.** The founding of New Orleans in 1718 marks the practical beginning of surviving organized record-keeping. Earlier events are rarely documented.

---

### Recommended Research Path

1. **Start at FamilySearch** with [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — this is the indexed entry point for colonial baptisms, marriages, and burials.
2. **Check probate** via [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) for the 1756–1769 window.
3. **Visit or contact the Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) for Superior Council records.
4. **Search the New Orleans Notarial Archives** for contracts, wills, and marriage settlements from the 1730s onward.
5. **Search ANOM online** (anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr) for colonial census rolls and administrative records — especially for settlers, soldiers, and officials.
6. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki** article "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records" for additional source leads as collections are continually digitized.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (Late 1800s, c. 1870–1905)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Primary region:** Pennsylvania's **anthracite coal region** (northeastern PA) — Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Luzerne County, Lackawanna County (formed from Luzerne in 1878), Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia counties; and the **bituminous coal region** (western PA) — Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, and Washington counties.
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state since 1787)
- **Population:** No population data was returned by the tool for this fixture; the Wikipedia Coal Region article notes that the anthracite region attracted massive immigrant populations from the 1820s onward, accelerating through the 1870s–1900s.
- **Economy:** Dominated by coal extraction — anthracite in the northeast, bituminous in the west. Mining companies controlled housing (company towns), stores, and employment, generating distinctive company-level records.
- **Ethnic composition (from Wikipedia Coal Region article):** Irish, Welsh, German (earlier waves); Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, Ukrainian (later waves, especially 1880s–1900s). Each group typically formed its own ethnic parish.
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, German Lutheran/Reformed, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Slovak/Ruthenian Greek Catholic, Ukrainian Orthodox, Italian Catholic, and various Protestant sects.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1876–1877, Schuylkill Co.); Great Railroad Strike (1877); founding of United Mine Workers of America (1890); Lattimer Massacre (1897, Luzerne Co.); continuous labor unrest generating court and newspaper records throughout the period.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County formed 1878** from the northern portion of Luzerne County. Scranton, Carbondale, and surrounding mining towns were in Luzerne County before that date. **Pre-1878 records for the Scranton/Carbondale area were filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne County first for events before 1878, then Lackawanna for 1878 onward.**
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811 and covers the central anthracite fields continuously through the target period.
- Carbon County (formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton) covers the southern anthracite fields; its pre-1843 records are in Monroe and Northampton counties.
- For the bituminous west, Allegheny County (Pittsburgh area) was well-established and stable throughout the period.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide birth and death registration until **1906**. A brief earlier attempt (1893–1905) produced incomplete returns. **For the late 1800s, civil vital records are largely absent at the state level.**
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 — 4,218,763 records with images on FamilySearch (indexed + images). Though it begins after the period, it captures deaths of people born and living through the 1870s–1900s, often recording birthplace, parents, and informant.
- **Marriage records:** County-level marriage licenses were issued; coverage varies. FamilySearch holds:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — 524,189 records with images (**indexed + images**)
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — 312,045 records with images (**indexed + images**)
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — 198,765 records, no images (**indexed, images not digitized**)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in the late 1800s must be sought through church records, census mortality schedules, and newspaper notices — not civil registration.

### Church Records ⚑ ESSENTIAL FOR THIS PERIOD
- **Denominations present:** See ethnic composition above. Ethnic parishes were the primary record-keepers for mining families in the late 1800s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, first communions. Ethnic parishes often recorded national origin and village of birth — invaluable for tracing immigrants to their home country.
- **Key collection:** *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* — 1,245,830 records, 607,220 images on FamilySearch (**indexed + images**). Covers many Protestant and some Catholic parishes across the state.
- **Language:** Non-English records are common. Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, Italian, and Welsh-language registers require reading in the original. Latin was used in Catholic sacramental formulae.
- **Gaps:** Many ethnic Catholic parishes (especially founded post-1880) have records still held by individual parishes or diocesan archives, not yet microfilmed or digitized. Contact the Diocese of Scranton (northeastern PA) or Diocese of Allentown (Schuylkill area) directly.
- **FamilySearch wiki note** (from "Pennsylvania Occupational Records" article): "Church records are essential — ethnic parishes (Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic) served specific mining communities and their registers often contain the most detailed family data."

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 are the key enumerations for this period. The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed** (fire, 1921) — it is almost entirely unavailable.
- **Occupation column:** Mining families appear with occupations like "miner," "mine laborer," "mine boss," "breaker boy." The 1880 census also lists industry.
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** Record deaths in the year preceding each census — particularly useful for identifying mining accident victims before state death certificates began.
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and searchable on Ancestry.com (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch.

### Occupational Records ⚑ DISTINCTIVE TO MINING COMMUNITIES
- **Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Mines published annual reports listing **fatal accidents by name, age, nationality, and cause of death**. Available at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). These are among the most valuable sources for identifying miners by nationality and locating them in the records. (Source: Wikipedia Coal Region article; FamilySearch "Pennsylvania Occupational Records" wiki.)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill Co., 1870–1900):** FamilySearch volume 002240015 — **410 images, 95% name-indexed, full-text searchable** (**indexed + images**). A strong starting point for Schuylkill County miners.
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne Co., 1870–1895):** FamilySearch volume 002240016 — **287 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** (**browse-only images**). Must be browsed image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna Co., 1878–1900):** FamilySearch volume 002240017 — **199 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** (**browse-only images**). Must be browsed image by image.
- **Note:** The volume search returned a total of 23 results (first page shown); additional mining-related volumes may be on subsequent pages.
- **Company employment records:** Mining companies maintained pay ledgers, accident reports, and employment cards. These survive **fragmentarily** at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. (Source: FamilySearch wiki.)
- **UMWA records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) maintained membership rolls and grievance files. Contact the UMWA archives or the Penn State University Special Collections (which holds significant labor records).

### Probate and Court Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* — 893,214 records with 446,607 images (**indexed + images**).
- **Court records:** Naturalizations (pre-1906) filed in county courts of record — Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, Orphans' Court. These contain declarations of intent and petitions for citizenship that often list age, birthplace, and immigration date.
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906):** Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** per the FamilySearch wiki.
- **Molly Maguires trials:** Court records from the 1876–1877 prosecutions in Schuylkill County name hundreds of Irish miners. Held at the Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Land Records
- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was not distributed by federal rectangular survey).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages. In company towns, miners often rented from the coal company rather than owning land, so deed records may be sparse for the working-class population. Tax records and company housing lists may be more informative.
- **Access:** County recorder of deeds (at each county courthouse). Deed indexes often online via county websites; images vary.

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many miners served. Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (available via Fold3, subscription); Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Civil War pension files** are particularly valuable — they contain affidavits from neighbors and relatives that can document family relationships and places of birth.
- **Access:** Fold3.com (subscription) for federal service/pension records; NARA (archives.gov) for in-person or mail requests.

### Cemetery Records
- **Major cemeteries:** Each ethnic community typically maintained its own burial ground, often adjacent to the parish church. Polish National Catholic, Lithuanian, Slovak, Welsh, and Irish Catholic cemeteries dot the coal region.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — free, crowd-sourced headstone photographs. Coverage is uneven; rural and ethnic-parish cemeteries are often underrepresented.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, when they survive, are held by the individual parish or cemetery association.

### Newspaper Records
- **Local papers:** The coal region had a dense newspaper landscape. Key titles include the *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill Co., from 1825) and the *Scranton Tribune*. Ethnic-language papers (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) also circulated.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, accident reports, coroner's inquests, marriage notices, labor news, and legal notices. Accident reporting in mining papers often names victims with nationality and survivors.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds many Pennsylvania papers. The State Library of Pennsylvania (Harrisburg) and local historical societies hold microfilm of regional titles not yet digitized.

### Immigration and Naturalization
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Ellis Island from 1892, Castle Garden before that).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA, searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intent and naturalization petitions filed in county courts.
- **Naturalization tip:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — check Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal courts for the county. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives (FamilySearch wiki).
- **FamilySearch wiki note:** "Many miners immigrated through the ports of Philadelphia and New York and naturalized in county courts near the mines."
- **Note on passenger lists:** The full arrival manifest lists every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full page for all accompanying family members.

### Tax Records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax lists. In the absence of 1890 census data and with late civil registration, tax lists serve as a substitute annual "census" to track a family year by year.
- **Where held:** County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch.

### School and Institutional Records
- **Breaker boys:** Child labor was common in mines. School enrollment records (held at county/district level) and child labor inspection records may document children in mining families.
- **Company store records:** Mining companies operated stores on a credit (truck) system. Store ledgers, when they survive, name employees and their dependents.
- **Hospital/accident records:** Mining injuries were frequent. Hospital admission records, when they survive, are held by individual institutions.

---

## Repository Guide

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not** in any major online database and require direct contact with the holding repository:

- Most ethnic Catholic parish registers (especially post-1880 parishes not yet microfilmed)
- Mining company employment records not covered by the FamilySearch volumes above
- Company store (truck system) ledgers
- Hospital and accident records
- UMWA membership rolls and grievance files
- Many local newspaper runs not yet digitized (especially ethnic-language papers)
- Pennsylvania State Police records (from 1905, used against striking miners)

---

## Known Record Gaps

- **1890 federal census:** Almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire. Use 1880 and 1900 census plus tax records to bridge the gap.
- **Statewide birth and death certificates:** Not required until 1906. The 1893–1905 registration attempt was incomplete. Church records are the only substitute for this period.
- **Mining company records:** Many companies destroyed or abandoned records when mines closed or companies reorganized. Survival is fragmentary and location-dependent.
- **Ethnic parish records:** Some parishes have not preserved or shared early registers. Contact individual parishes or diocesan archives.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Mine Inspector Reports** if you know a miner died on the job — they name victims by name, age, and nationality from 1870 onward, held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
2. **Lackawanna County boundary split:** Any event in the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 is filed under Luzerne County — always check Luzerne first for pre-1878 events in that area.
3. **Identify the ethnic parish first.** Because civil vital records are absent for this period, the ethnic parish register is often the only source for births, marriages, and deaths. Knowing the nationality narrows the denomination: Irish → Catholic; Welsh → Congregational or Baptist; Polish/Slovak/Lithuanian → Catholic; Ukrainian → Greek Catholic or Orthodox.
4. **Use census occupation + birthplace columns together.** In 1880 and 1900, "miner" plus a foreign birthplace column immediately suggests an immigrant chain-migration community. Check neighbors on the same census page for family connections.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Search Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal district court records — not just one court — for the county where your ancestor lived.
6. **Non-English records require language skills.** Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, Italian, and Welsh registers were kept in the heritage language. FamilySearch's translation tools or a specialist may be needed.
7. **Company town records vary wildly.** Some mining companies (e.g., Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company) maintained detailed employment records; others did not. The Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies are the first inquiry points.
8. **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville)** is one of the longest-running and most genealogically rich coal-region newspapers — it reported accidents, inquests, and local notices in detail from the 1820s onward. Check Newspapers.com and the State Library of Pennsylvania for holdings.
9. **For the 1890 census gap**, supplement with the 1885 Pennsylvania state census (where it survives for your county), tax lists, city directories, and church registers to place families in the early 1890s.
10. **UMWA records (from 1890):** If your ancestor was an organized miner after 1890, Penn State's Special Collections holds significant UMWA materials that may include membership and grievance records.
