# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Key polities:** Two separate colonies co-existed for most of this period: **Plymouth Colony** (est. 1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (est. 1628). They remained legally distinct until 1691, when they merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay**.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England (Crown charter); from 1691, a royal province.
- **Population:** The Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers arrived between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia: *Massachusetts Bay Colony*). No population census data is available through FamilySearch for this pre-federal period.
- **Religious denominations:** Overwhelmingly Congregationalist (Puritan). The Congregational church was the established church of the colony.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630–1640); King Philip's War (1675–1676); Salem witch crisis (1692); charter revocation and royal province formation (1691).

---

## ⚠️ Critical boundary note

**Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony are two entirely separate jurisdictions.** Their records are held, indexed, and published separately. Before searching any record type, determine which colony your ancestor lived in:

- **Plymouth Colony** (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties): Records are published and indexed as a distinct corpus. The *Plymouth Colony Records* are published separately and cover 1620–1691.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, etc.): Massachusetts Archives, Boston.
- After **1691**: Both colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay — records converge under one jurisdiction.

---

## Available record types

### 1. Vital Records (Civil Registration) ★ PRIMARY SOURCE
- **Start date:** 1639 — Massachusetts is one of the earliest jurisdictions in the Americas to mandate civil vital registration. Town clerks were required to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning that year (FamilySearch Wiki: *Massachusetts Genealogy*).
- **What exists:** Town-level births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward.
- **Published compilations:** The **Tanner–Corbin series** (*Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850*) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. This is typically the first place to check.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (Collection ID: 2061550) — 3,456,789 records with 1,728,394 images. **Indexed + images.** Search at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Physical originals:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston; individual town clerks.
- **Gaps:** Coverage is by town — confirm your ancestor's town first. Some early records were not consistently kept or have been lost.

### 2. Church Records ★ PRIMARY SOURCE
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (dominant); small numbers of Quakers (especially southeastern MA), Baptists, and Anglicans.
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Because Congregational churches were the established church of the colony, church membership and civil life were tightly intertwined — these records capture events that appear nowhere else.
- **Published sources:** Many early church records have been published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and local historical society publications (FamilySearch Wiki: *Massachusetts Church Records*).
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (Collection ID: 1921657) — 987,654 records with 493,827 images. **Indexed + images.** Search at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Physical originals:** Individual church archives; Massachusetts Archives; NEHGS (New England Historic Genealogical Society), Boston.

### 3. Probate Records ★ HIGH VALUE
- **Date range:** 1635 onward — county probate courts kept records nearly from the colony's founding.
- **Content:** Wills, estate inventories, administration files, guardianships. Inventories are especially rich for this period, listing every household item and debt.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (Collection ID: 1678901) — 567,890 records with 283,945 images. **Indexed + images.** Search at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Physical originals:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives.
- **Plymouth quirk:** Plymouth Colony probate records are separate — see *Plymouth Colony Records*.

### 4. Land Records
- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (not rectangular survey).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents. County registries of deeds have been recording deeds from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (FamilySearch Wiki: *Massachusetts Genealogy*).
- **Where held:** County Registries of Deeds (physical); some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Access:** Land records are not covered by a dedicated FamilySearch indexed collection for this period — check county-level registries and published abstracts (e.g., the Suffolk Deeds series is published in full for the 17th century).
- **Digitization level: Microfilm / physical** for most county deed books in this period.

### 5. Court Records
- **Types:** General Court (legislature/highest court), Court of Assistants, county courts, Quarterly Courts. Records include civil suits, criminal cases, and — critically for genealogy — oaths, freemen's lists, and town governance actions.
- **Plymouth Colony Records:** Published in 12 volumes (Nathaniel Shurtleff, ed.) covering 1620–1692 — includes general court proceedings, acts, land grants, and vital records. This published series is the key finding tool.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston. Some records transcribed and published (e.g., *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay in New England*, 5 vols.).
- **Digitization level: Physical and published compilations** — not fully indexed online.

### 6. Census / Enumerations
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census was 1790 — entirely outside this period. No federal census covers 1620–1700.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Tax lists, militia musters, and freemen's lists serve as census substitutes. These are recorded in colony court records and town records.
- **Specific substitute:** The **1643 and 1647 lists of able-bodied men** (militia records) survive for parts of Massachusetts Bay Colony and serve as a near-census of adult males.

### 7. Immigration / Passenger Records
- **FamilySearch collection note:** The **Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** collection (ID: 1784312) covers post-period immigration and does not apply to 1620–1700 arrivals.
- **For 17th-century arrivals:** The definitive resource is the **Great Migration Study Project** (NEHGS), which documents every known settler who arrived in New England between 1620 and 1643 in exhaustive biographical sketches with sources. The series runs to multiple volumes by Robert Charles Anderson.
- **Ship records:** Scattered among English port records, colonial newspapers, and family papers. Many have been abstracted in *The Great Migration Begins* (3 vols.) and the ongoing *Great Migration* series.
- **Digitization level:** Published print/digital series (NEHGS); not a standard searchable FamilySearch collection.

### 8. Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1676).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, service lists, pension petitions (King Philip's War pensions are particularly well documented). Some records appear in the published colony court records.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published in *The Soldiers and Sailors of the War of the Revolution* and similar volumes. Fold3.com holds some compiled military records.
- **Digitization level: Microfilm and physical** for original muster rolls; published abstracts available in print.

### 9. Cemetery Records
- **Character:** 17th-century Puritan burial grounds survive in many towns (e.g., Granary Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1660; Charter Street Cemetery, Salem, est. 1637). Many stones are still legible.
- **Published transcriptions:** The *Epitaphs from Graveyards in Wellesley, etc.* and similar town-by-town transcription projects exist for most old Massachusetts towns.
- **Online:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has coverage for many colonial burial grounds — check individual cemetery pages.
- **Sexton records:** Where they exist (mainly post-1700), held at town clerk offices.

### 10. Newspapers
- **Period coverage:** The first newspaper in British North America, *Publick Occurrences*, was published in Boston in 1690 (one issue only). The *Boston News-Letter* began 1704 — just outside this period.
- **Practical value:** Newspapers are not a meaningful source for the 1620–1700 period. Resort to court records and published genealogies for legal notices and death notices.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | What's Available for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Town Vital Records 1620–1890; Church Records 1630–1920; Probate Records 1635–1991 | Free |
| **NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org)** | Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; New England vital records database | Subscription (some free) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. census (post-1790 only, not applicable); some early MA vital records compilations | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Colonial burial grounds, many transcribed | Free |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Post-period records primarily; some colonial-era manuscript scans | Free/In-person |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from 1620s onward | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston** | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections; Great Migration series | In-person research library; subscription database online |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from 1630s onward by county | In-person; some microfilmed |
| **County Probate Courts** | Original probate files | In-person |
| **Individual town clerks** | Original vital record books | In-person or mail |
| **Congregational Library & Archives, Boston** | Congregational church records and minutes | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Records NOT online (for 1620–1700)

- **County deed books** — most must be consulted at county registries or on microfilm, though the Suffolk Deeds are published in print
- **Colony court records** — available in published transcriptions but the originals are at Massachusetts Archives
- **Militia muster rolls** — Massachusetts Archives; published abstracts in colonial era volumes
- **Individual town clerk volumes** — some digitized via FamilySearch; others still local only
- **Most Congregational church registers** — many unpublished, held at individual churches or NEHGS

---

## Known record losses

- **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** caused destruction of several town records in attacked frontier towns (e.g., Deerfield, Northfield, Brookfield). Check whether your ancestor's town was affected.
- **Plymouth Colony records** are largely intact but are a separate corpus from Massachusetts Bay — they were not integrated until after 1691.
- Some early town clerks were irregular in their recording before enforcement of the 1639 mandate improved; expect gaps in the 1639–1650 decade.

---

## Research tips

1. **Identify the colony first.** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony are separate jurisdictions with separate record streams. Determine which one your ancestor lived in before searching any record set.
2. **Search the Tanner–Corbin published vital records series first.** The *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series covers 200+ towns and is the fastest entry point for births, marriages, and deaths.
3. **The Great Migration Study (NEHGS) is essential for 1620–1643 arrivals.** If your ancestor arrived in the Great Migration, Robert Charles Anderson's biographical sketches (with exhaustive source citations) may solve problems that no individual record search can.
4. **Work at the town level, not the county level.** In this period, towns were the primary unit of record-keeping. Identify the specific town of residence — county is less useful.
5. **Church membership was civil documentation.** Admissions, dismissions, and disciplinary proceedings in Congregational records are equivalent to civil documentation for this population. Do not skip them.
6. **No federal census before 1790.** Substitute with: town tax lists, militia/muster rolls, freemen's lists, and the 1643/1647 able-bodied men lists found in colony court records.
7. **Plymouth Colony Records (12 vols., ed. Shurtleff) and Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay (5 vols.) are the published gateways to colony-level records.** Both are available at major research libraries and some are digitized.
8. **After 1691**, records unify under the Province of Massachusetts Bay — searches become simpler after that date.

---

## 🗺 Oklahoma Territory — Locality Research Guide
**Target period:** 1889 (Land Run) – c. 1920 (post-statehood)
**Standard place:** Oklahoma, United States

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Understanding Oklahoma's split administration before statehood is the single most important thing you can know before searching records.

| Period | Jurisdiction | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-April 22, 1889 | Indian Territory (all of present-day Oklahoma) | Federal/tribal, no non-Indian settlement |
| Apr 22, 1889 | Land Run opens the "Unassigned Lands" (Oklahoma District) | Settlers arrive; no civil government yet |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov 16, 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (west) + **Indian Territory** (east) | Two separate federal jurisdictions, administered independently |
| Nov 16, 1907 onward | **State of Oklahoma** | Both territories merged at statehood |

**The critical split:** Before 1907, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were legally distinct. A family in Guthrie or Oklahoma City was in Oklahoma Territory; a family in Muskogee or Tahlequah was in Indian Territory under tribal governance. The record systems are separate. **Identify which territory your ancestor lived in first**, then target the right record set.

---

### 1. Land Records — *The Top Priority for Land Run Research*

This is the primary record class for 1889-era settlers. Oklahoma is a **federal land state**, meaning the U.S. government issued all original land patents.

**FamilySearch collection — indexed + images:**
> **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907**
> Collection ID 1541872 · 234,567 records · 117,283 images
> [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)

**Beyond FamilySearch — two critical federal repositories:**

- **BLM General Land Office Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — Searchable online database of land patents. Free. Returns the patent itself with the legal land description, date, and patentee name.
- **National Archives, Washington D.C. — Record Group 49 (General Land Office)** — The *full homestead case file*, which is far richer than the patent alone. A complete file typically includes: the original application, proof-of-settlement affidavits with witnesses, the claimant's age and nativity, and sometimes letters from family members. **Rejected applications also survive** and can contain the most detailed family information. Request by legal land description.

> **Quirk:** Homestead contest files exist when a claim was disputed by another settler. These contain sworn depositions that frequently name family members, give prior residences, and describe the claimant's movements — an exceptional source when they exist.

---

### 2. Indian Censuses and Tribal Rolls

Essential for any family with Native American connections, and also for non-Native families in Indian Territory who interacted with tribal governments.

**FamilySearch collection — indexed + images:**
> **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959**
> Collection ID 1987432 · 567,890 records · 283,945 images
> [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)

Key sub-series within this record class:
- **Dawes Commission Enrollment Records (ca. 1898–1914)** — Enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole). Includes **Freedmen rolls** for formerly enslaved people of the tribes. These are among the most detailed family records for Indian Territory.
- Annual Indian censuses (various Five Civilized Tribes), held at the National Archives at Fort Worth.

---

### 3. Census Records

| Census | What Exists | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1890** | Oklahoma Territory *special census* (partial) | One of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the nation. Most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire. The Oklahoma Territory special census is held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**. |
| **1900** | Full federal census — Oklahoma Territory enumerated | Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **1907** | Oklahoma State census | Taken at statehood; held at Oklahoma State Archives |
| **1910** | Full federal census — State of Oklahoma | Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry |

> **Quirk:** The 1890 special census for Oklahoma Territory is one of your most important records for first-wave Land Run settlers and their families. Go to the Oklahoma Historical Society for access.

---

### 4. Marriage Records

Vital registration was **not mandatory** in Oklahoma Territory before statehood (1907). County marriage records are the most reliable territorial-era vital record.

**FamilySearch collection — indexed + images:**
> **Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995**
> Collection ID 2134789 · 456,789 records · 913,578 images
> [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)

> **Quirk:** For births and deaths in the 1889–1907 window, civil registration is sparse to nonexistent. Substitute sources: church registers, newspaper notices, census mortality schedules, and probate records.

---

### 5. Church and Mission Records

Churches were established almost immediately as new towns formed in 1889 — Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian missions in particular. Earlier mission records reach back to the 1820s for Indian Territory.

**FamilySearch collection — indexed + images:**
> **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965**
> Collection ID 1654321 · 123,456 records · 61,728 images
> [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)

For congregation-level records not on FamilySearch, contact denominational archives directly (e.g., Oklahoma United Methodist Archives, Baptist archives).

---

### 6. Territorial Court Records

Territorial courts (1890–1907) handled civil and criminal cases, probate, and — critically — **naturalizations**. Pre-September 1906, naturalization could occur in any court of record; after the Basic Naturalization Act of September 1906, it was federalized.

- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — Holds Oklahoma Territory district court records (Record Group for territorial courts), including naturalization petitions and final papers.
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) — District court records continuing into the state period.

> *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Territorial Records," section "Territorial Courts and Early Settlement")*

---

### 7. Military Records

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Civil War service & pension files | National Archives, Washington D.C. | Pension files often document pre-Oklahoma origin state |
| Spanish-American War (1898) | National Archives / Fold3 | Oklahoma Territory raised volunteer units |
| WWI Draft Registrations (1917–18) | NARA / Ancestry / FamilySearch | Captures men who settled in Oklahoma in the 1890s–1900s |
| State adjutant general records | Oklahoma State Archives | —|

**Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://fold3.com)) — subscription site with military records curated for genealogy research.

---

### 8. Newspapers

Oklahoma territorial newspapers began publishing in April–May 1889, within days of the Land Run. They carried homestead notices, legal advertisements, social notices, and obituaries.

- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://newspapers.com)) — subscription; holds many territorial Oklahoma papers
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — holds territorial newspaper microfilm including the *Oklahoma State Capital* (Guthrie) and others
- *Chronicles of Oklahoma* (OHS journal) — useful for historical context and published family histories

---

### 9. Tracing Origins — Where Did They Come From?

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Oklahoma Territorial Records"), Land Run settlers came disproportionately from **Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and Tennessee**. To find where your ancestor was before 1889:

- Search the 1880 federal census in those states (most Land Run settlers would appear there)
- Check Civil War pension files (often state the applicant's origin)
- Review homestead case files for nativity statements
- County histories published c. 1900–1920 often include biographical sketches with origin information

---

### 10. Additional Online Repositories

The following external resources were returned for Oklahoma, 1889–1920:

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **Ancestry.com** — [ancestry.com](https://ancestry.com) | U.S. federal census collection (1900, 1910); Oklahoma-specific databases |
| **Find A Grave** — [findagrave.com](https://findagrave.com) | Cemetery records; many early settler graves documented |
| **Fold3** — [fold3.com](https://fold3.com) | Military records |
| **Newspapers.com** — [newspapers.com](https://newspapers.com) | Territorial-era Oklahoma newspapers |
| **NARA** — [archives.gov](https://archives.gov) | Federal records; contact the National Archives at Fort Worth for territorial-era holdings |
| **BLM GLO Records** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Free, searchable land patents |

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Oklahoma Territory territorial court records, Indian Territory records, tribal records | In-person or NARA request |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | RG 49 homestead case files, military pension files | Written/online request |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)**, Oklahoma City | 1890 special census, territorial newspapers, county histories, state records | In-person; some digitized |
| **Oklahoma State Archives**, Oklahoma City | District court records (post-1907), state vital records post-1907, legislative records | In-person |
| **BLM GLO Records** | All federal land patents, free and searchable | glorecords.blm.gov |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 confirmed collections covering land records, Indian rolls, marriages, church records | Free at familysearch.org |

---

### Critical Research Quirks at a Glance

1. **Two-territory split:** Before statehood (1907), Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) were separate jurisdictions with separate record systems. Identify which territory your ancestor was in before choosing a record set.
2. **The 1890 census gap:** The national 1890 census was largely destroyed, but Oklahoma Territory's special census (1890) is one of the rare survivors — held at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
3. **Homestead files are richer than patents:** The full case file at NARA (RG 49) contains settlement proof affidavits, nativity, family details, and witnesses — far more than the land patent itself.
4. **No statewide vital registration before 1907:** For 1889–1907, rely on county marriage records (earliest start around 1890), church registers, newspaper notices, and census substitutes for births and deaths.
5. **Dawes Rolls are essential for Indian Territory families:** The Dawes Commission enrollment records (ca. 1898–1914) are the key genealogical source for Five Civilized Tribes members and their Freedmen.
6. **Naturalizations before Sept. 1906 appear in territorial courts:** Check National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives, not just federal immigration records.
7. **Trace origins in departure states:** Search 1880 records in Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and Tennessee to find your ancestor before the Land Run.

## 📍 Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region — Pre-Statehood, c. 1790–1819

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Around 1800, the land that is now Alabama did not yet exist as its own jurisdiction. It passed through three overlapping administrative layers, and records follow those layers — not the eventual state of Alabama:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| To 1763 | French Louisiana (Mobile district) | Mobile founded 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish West Florida (Mobile District) | Spain held Mobile until U.S. seizure |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** | Alabama was the *eastern* half of this territory |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** | Split from Mississippi Territory |
| From Dec. 14, 1819 | **State of Alabama** | |

**County formation was rapid and critically important.** Most of present-day Alabama was initially organized as **Washington County (1800)**. Madison County was carved out in 1808, Baldwin County in 1809, and Mobile County in 1812. Which county held authority over a given event determines where court, probate, and land records are filed. You must trace county boundaries before searching.

> **Critical search rule:** Pre-statehood Alabama records were created under *Mississippi Territory* (before 1817) and then *Alabama Territory* (1817–1819). On FamilySearch, search under **Mississippi** as well as **Alabama** for any event before December 1819. The two sets are not duplicates — they are a single continuous research trail split across two filing jurisdictions.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 🏛️ Census & Population Lists

**Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816)** enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama under the Mississippi Territory administration. These are among the most valuable substitutes for the destroyed 1790–1810 federal censuses for this region.

- **Repository:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson. These are physical/microfilm holdings — not currently online as browsable or indexed volumes.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* (Collection 2016756) — 287,634 indexed records, **no images**. Index only; images must be obtained from ADAH/MDAH directly.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* (Collection 1927171) — 198,340 indexed records, **no images**. Overlaps the territorial period and includes Alabama enumerations.
- **1810 Federal Census** exists for Mississippi Territory (covering Alabama) and is available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

**Digitization gap:** Volume search returned **zero** digitized, browsable image volumes specifically tagged to the Alabama/Mississippi area for 1790–1820. Territorial census originals remain physical-only at state archives.

---

#### 🌾 Land Records — *Prime source for this period*

Federal land sales in the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory began in **1803**, administered through two land offices:

- **St. Stephens Land Office** (southern Alabama / Tombigbee district)
- **Huntsville Land Office** (northern Alabama / Tennessee Valley)

Federal land entry case files are held at **NARA (Record Group 49)**. Original patents are **indexed and searchable by name** on the **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website** at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — this is the best digitized, freely searchable resource for the period.

Spanish and British land grants in the Mobile area predate U.S. administration and are held separately (see Colonial Records below).

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* (Collection 1919694) — 312,450 records, 156,225 images. Covers the territorial period and includes Alabama-area transactions filed under the Mississippi Territory.

---

#### 👨‍⚖️ Probate & Court Records

Territorial courts functioned from the earliest American settlement. Washington County court records (from 1800) are the primary source for probate and civil proceedings covering most of present-day Alabama before later counties formed.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (Collection 1537764) — 438,210 records, 219,105 images. The earliest records in this collection begin in 1809, aligning with the later county formations.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (Collection 1855293) — 245,670 records, 122,835 images. Territorial-era court records (1799 onward) that include the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.

> **Quirk:** Court and probate records for events before 1808–1812 in most of present-day Alabama will appear under *Washington County, Mississippi Territory* — not under any Alabama county. Search the Mississippi collection first for pre-county-formation events.

---

#### 💍 Marriage Records

Civil marriage registration in the Alabama counties began as counties formed (Madison 1808, Baldwin 1809, Mobile 1812, etc.). There are no territorial-level marriage records predating county formation — church registers are the only source for that window.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (Collection 1598408) — 612,345 records, 306,172 images. Earliest records start 1809 in the earliest-formed counties.

---

#### ⛪ Church Records

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are especially critical for this period, as civil registration was sparse and territorial census survival is limited.

- **Catholic records (Mobile area):** The Catholic Diocese of Mobile was the dominant institution. Sacramental registers from the colonial period through early statehood survive, some dating to the French and Spanish periods. Originals at the Archdiocese of Mobile; microfilm copies at ADAH and FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (Collection 1986396) — 156,789 records, 78,394 images. Includes Baptist, Methodist, and Catholic congregations.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950* (Collection 2034891) — 87,654 records, 43,827 images. May include records from congregations straddling the territorial boundary.

> **Quirk:** Catholic sacramental registers for the Mobile district are partially in **French and Spanish** — researchers must read the original language. Indexes where they exist may not cover every entry; browse the images for the full record.

---

#### 🪖 Military Records

- **Militia rolls** (Mississippi Territory): The territorial militia enrolled free male residents and is a valuable census substitute. Held at ADAH and MDAH. Not currently digitized as browsable volumes on FamilySearch.
- **Creek War (1813–1814) service records:** At NARA; indexed on Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://fold3.com)).
- **War of 1812 pension files:** At NARA; searchable on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Bounty land warrants** for service were a major vehicle for land acquisition in Alabama — cross-reference with the BLM GLO land records.

---

#### 🗺️ Colonial Records (Mobile District) — Pre-1798

If your ancestor was in the Mobile area before American territorial control, three archival bodies hold the primary records:

| Records | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **French colonial records** (1702–1763) | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | Physical; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **Spanish colonial records** (1780–1813): censuses, church registers, land grants | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Physical; copies at Library of Congress |
| **British West Florida** (1763–1780) | British National Archives; Library of Congress | Physical/microfilm |

These are largely **not digitized as browsable online volumes**. Contact the Mobile Municipal Archives or ADAH for microfilm access.

---

#### 📰 Newspapers

The *Mobile Gazette* (est. 1813) is the earliest Alabama newspaper and carries land notices, estate notices, and legal advertisements — effectively a substitute for some vital and court records. Check [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) and the Library of Congress *Chronicling America* project for early digitized Alabama papers.

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH)**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses, early county records, military rosters, church microfilm | On-site + some online finding aids |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History (MDAH)**, Jackson | Mississippi Territory records including Alabama portion | On-site |
| **NARA** (Atlanta regional + Washington D.C.) | Federal land entry files (RG 49), military records | On-site + online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **BLM GLO website** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, indexed, free | Fully online, name-searchable |
| **FamilySearch** | Collections listed above | Online, mixed index+image |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | French colonial microfilm | On-site |
| **Archdiocese of Mobile Archives** | Catholic sacramental registers | On-site/by request |

---

### Digitized & Browsable Volumes — Summary Assessment

The user specifically asked about this. Here is an honest accounting:

| Record Type | Digitized Browsable Volumes on FamilySearch? |
|---|---|
| Territorial censuses (1801–1816) | ❌ No — physical/microfilm only at ADAH and MDAH |
| Federal land patents | ✅ Yes — BLM GLO website, fully name-searchable |
| County marriages (from 1809) | ✅ Indexed + images on FamilySearch (Col. 1598408) |
| County probate (from 1809) | ✅ Indexed + images on FamilySearch (Col. 1537764) |
| Miss. Territory court records | ✅ Indexed + images on FamilySearch (Col. 1855293) |
| Miss. Territory land records | ✅ Indexed + images on FamilySearch (Col. 1919694) |
| Church records | ✅ Partially — FamilySearch (Col. 1986396 & 2034891); Catholic originals on-site |
| Militia rolls | ❌ No — physical/microfilm at ADAH |
| Colonial records (French/Spanish) | ❌ No — European archives; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |

**FamilySearch volume search returned zero specifically tagged pre-statehood Alabama/Mississippi Territory image volumes for 1790–1820** — this is a genuine digitization gap. The collections listed above do contain images for early records within their date ranges, but there are no standalone browse-only image volumes appearing for this territorial window. For the most granular browsing, you would need to work through the early image sets within the Alabama and Mississippi indexed collections above, or go to ADAH directly.

---

### Key Research Quirks

1. **Search under "Mississippi" at FamilySearch for any event before December 1819** — records created during the Mississippi Territory period (1798–1817) are filed under Mississippi, not Alabama.
2. **Trace county boundaries before searching** — most of present-day Alabama was Washington County (Mississippi Territory) before 1808–1812. The county that held jurisdiction determines where the record is filed.
3. **No statewide vital registration existed** in this period. Church registers and county marriage bonds are the only vital-record substitutes.
4. **The Mobile district has a distinct colonial paper trail** in European archives (French and Spanish) that is largely inaccessible online.
5. **Catholic records in the Mobile area may be in French or Spanish** — plan to read originals rather than relying on translated indexes.
6. **Federal land records are the best-indexed, most accessible source** for this period — start at BLM GLO before FamilySearch for land-related research.
7. **Territorial census survival is incomplete** — combine with tax lists and militia rolls (ADAH) for population coverage.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)
**Counties:** Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia
**Project:** Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908, Schuylkill County)

---

## Jurisdiction overview

Six counties in east-central Pennsylvania form the anthracite coal field. **Schuylkill County** (the county most directly relevant to your project) was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; it is the best-documented county at the FamilySearch level for this region. Population there boomed rapidly — from **89,510 in 1860** to **116,428 in 1870**, **129,974 in 1880**, and **172,927 by 1900** — driven entirely by anthracite mining. FamilySearch's population notes explicitly call out a *large immigrant population including Irish, Welsh, and German from the 1840s onward*.

Economy was colliery work: loaders, breaker boys, mule drivers, and miners. Dominant faith was Roman Catholic, with parishes established 1840–1870 to serve Irish (and later Eastern European) immigrant communities.

---

## Boundary changes — one critical quirk

| County | Formation | Quirk |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill | 1811 (from Berks + Northampton) | Stable through 1860–1900 |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878 (from Luzerne)** | **Pre-1878 Scranton/Carbondale records are in Luzerne County — search Luzerne first** |
| Carbon, Luzerne, Northumberland, Columbia | Various | FamilySearch resolves these to state level only — use **"Pennsylvania, United States"** as the standardPlace for volume/collection searches |

---

## Available record types

### ⭐ Coal-region specialized indexes — start here for miners
*(FamilySearch Wiki: "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" — page read in full)*

| Index | Coverage | What it contains |
|---|---|---|
| **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** | 1855–1898, ~41,000 workers | Colliery worker names from payroll books; includes **occupation** (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and **parish of origin** where stated. Drawn from records that survived a 1903 consolidation. |
| **Mine inspection / accident reports** | Ongoing | Organized by **colliery, not by person** — not a name-finding aid; don't rely on these for immigrant identification |
| **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments** | From 1853 | List householder, real estate value, occupation, and **sometimes nativity** — valuable substitute for the destroyed 1890 census |

> The wiki is explicit: *payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.* Use the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index before anything else.

---

### ⭐ Naturalization records — critical for proving Irish origin

| Volume / Collection | Images / Records | Indexed? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill Co. Naturalization Records, 1849–1915 (vol. 007936750) | 298 images | **0% — browse-only** | Declarations + petitions; name country of origin; must be browsed image by image |
| PA state Naturalization Records, 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443) | 351 images | **15% name-indexed** | English + German; run a name search first, then browse |

- **Pre-September 1906:** Naturalization scattered across county courts — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts all had jurisdiction (FamilySearch wiki, "Pennsylvania Naturalization Records"). Try all three court series.
- **After September 1906:** Centralized in federal courts; NARA Philadelphia holds eastern Pennsylvania records.

---

### Church records — primary source for births and pre-1906 deaths

| Diocese of Scranton archives | Unquantified | Physical | Baptismal registers for coal-region Catholic parishes, **1868 onward** |
| Diocese of Harrisburg archives | Unquantified | Physical | Baptismal registers for coal-region Catholic parishes, **before 1868** |

> The wiki notes Catholic parishes in the coal region were established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants. The Diocese of Scranton / Diocese of Harrisburg split at 1868 is the key access rule for Irish Catholic families.

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

**Deaths:**

- Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (coll. 2255317, 4,218,763 records): **indexed + images** — starts at 1906, so it postdates most of the 1860–1900 window but will catch miners who died after 1906 (relevant for Patrick Flynn, who died 1908 in Schuylkill County).

- **1890 federal census** population schedules are mostly destroyed nationwide. Substitute: triennial state tax assessments (1853 onward, sometimes record nativity) and church registers.

## Research tips — ordered by priority

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first.** ~41,000 colliery workers with occupation and parish of origin — the single best finding aid for Irish immigrant miners in the anthracite field.
2. **Pre-1878 Scranton/Carbondale area: search Luzerne County.** Lackawanna County didn't exist until 1878.
3. **Naturalization records can prove Irish birth.** Try the 15%-indexed PA state naturalization volume first; then browse Schuylkill Co.'s 298 images. Declarations of intent and petitions name country of origin.
4. **Diocese of Scranton (1868+) / Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868) for Catholic registers.** The diocesan split at 1868 governs where baptismal registers are held for coal-region parishes.
5. **1880 census is the highest-priority census.** First to record household relationships; foundational for proving family structure.
6. **Triennial tax assessments bridge the destroyed 1890 census.** Sometimes record nativity — useful for distinguishing Irish-born from American-born family members.
7. **Expect name anglicization.** Irish names were frequently anglicized; search under both Irish and English forms, and expect spelling variation between mine payroll records and church registers.
8. **Mine inspection/accident reports are by colliery, not by name.** Don't rely on them as a name-finding tool.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)
**Counties:** Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia
**Audience:** Researchers tracing Irish immigrant miners

---

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Region:** Six counties in east-central Pennsylvania forming the anthracite coal field: Schuylkill, Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Columbia.
- **Schuylkill County formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States (state since 1787).
- **Population — Schuylkill County** (FamilySearch population data; rapid growth attributed to anthracite coal mining, large immigrant population including Irish, Welsh, and German from 1840s onward):
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  - 1900: 172,927
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery occupations including loader, breaker boy, and mule driver.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, German immigrants from the 1840s; Eastern European communities arrived later in the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities — Diocese of Scranton (1868 onward); Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868).

---

## Boundary changes
- **Schuylkill County:** Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; stable during 1860–1900.
- **Lackawanna County:** Carved from Luzerne County in 1878. Pre-1878 records for the Scranton/Carbondale area are filed under **Luzerne County** — search Luzerne first for any event before 1878.
- FamilySearch's place database resolves Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Columbia counties to the state-level standardPlace "Pennsylvania, United States" — use that standardPlace when running collection and volume searches for those five counties.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

**Deaths:**
- Pennsylvania state death records volume (008120442, 674 images, 1852–1968): **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records): **indexed + images** — postdates most of the target window; useful for miners who lived past 1906.

**Marriages:**
- Schuylkill County marriage volume (007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records): **indexed + images** — covers the end of the target period.
- Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records): **indexed + images**.
- Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records): **indexed, no images**.

**Births:** No dedicated birth certificate collection covering 1860–1900 surfaced in tool results. Church baptismal registers are the primary source.

---

### Church records ⭐ Primary source for vital events

- Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985 (collection 1401638, 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons): **indexed + images** — broadest searchable Pennsylvania church record collection.
- Schuylkill County church records volume (007936751, 187 images, 1842–1895, English/German): **browse-only** — 0% indexed; bilingual — identify the record language before reading.
- **Catholic parish registers (coal-region specific):** Per the FamilySearch wiki ("Pennsylvania Coal Region Records"), many Catholic parishes were established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants. Baptismal registers are held by:
  - **Diocese of Scranton** — events from 1868 onward
  - **Diocese of Harrisburg** — events before 1868

---

### Census records

- Federal censuses for 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 cover all coal counties. The **1890 population schedules are mostly destroyed** — substitute with triennial state tax assessments.
- The **1880 census** is the first to record household member relationships — highest priority for proving family structure.
- The 1870 and 1900 censuses provide complementary evidence for families with children present (FamilySearch wiki).

---

### Probate records

- Schuylkill County probate volume (007936749, 412 images, 1851–1930): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania state probate volume (008120441, 1,180 images, 1683–1994): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 893,214 records): **indexed + images**.

---

### Naturalization records ⭐ Critical for Irish immigrants

- Schuylkill County naturalization volume (007936750, 298 images, 1849–1915): **browse-only** — 0% indexed. Declarations of intent and petitions name country of origin; must be browsed image by image.
- Pennsylvania state naturalization volume (008120443, 351 images, 1790–1915, English/German): **15% name-indexed** — run a name search before browsing.
- **Pre-1906:** Records scattered among county Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts (FamilySearch wiki, "Pennsylvania Naturalization Records").
- **After September 1906:** Centralized in federal courts; NARA Philadelphia for eastern Pennsylvania.

---

### Land and deed records

- Schuylkill County deed records volume (007936752, 543 images, 1815–1900): **22% name-indexed** — partially searchable; the most accessible Schuylkill County volume by name search.

---

### Military records

- The Civil War (1861–1865) falls within the target period. Pennsylvania service records, pension files, and draft registrations are held at NARA. State adjutant general records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### Coal-region specialized indexes ⭐ Key for miner ancestors
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records")*

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** ~41,000 colliery workers named, drawn from company payroll books. Entries include occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin where stated — the most direct finding aid for Irish immigrant miners.
2. **Mine inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less useful for name lookups; use payroll-derived indexes first.
3. **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853:** List householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census.

---

### Tax records

- Triennial state assessments from 1853 cover coal-region residents; sometimes record nativity (FamilySearch wiki).
- Ancestry: Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 — pre-period, useful for establishing earlier family presence.

---

### Newspapers

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)
**Counties:** Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia
**Audience:** Researchers tracing Irish immigrant miners

---

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Region:** Six counties in east-central Pennsylvania forming the anthracite coal field: Schuylkill, Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Columbia.
- **Schuylkill County formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States (state since 1787).
- **Population — Schuylkill County** (FamilySearch population data; rapid growth attributed to anthracite coal mining, large immigrant population including Irish, Welsh, and German from 1840s onward):
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  - 1900: 172,927
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery occupations including loader, breaker boy, and mule driver.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, German immigrants from the 1840s; Eastern European communities arrived later in the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities — Diocese of Scranton (1868 onward); Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868).

---

## Boundary changes
- **Schuylkill County:** Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; stable during 1860–1900.
- **Lackawanna County:** Carved from Luzerne County in 1878. Pre-1878 records for the Scranton/Carbondale area are filed under **Luzerne County** — search Luzerne first for any event before 1878.
- FamilySearch's place database resolves Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Columbia counties to the state-level standardPlace "Pennsylvania, United States" — use that standardPlace when running collection and volume searches for those five counties.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

**Deaths:**
- Pennsylvania state death records volume (008120442, 674 images, 1852–1968): **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records): **indexed + images** — postdates most of the target window; useful for miners who lived past 1906.

**Marriages:**
- Schuylkill County marriage volume (007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records): **indexed + images** — covers the end of the target period.
- Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records): **indexed + images**.
- Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records): **indexed, no images**.

**Births:** No dedicated birth certificate collection covering 1860–1900 surfaced in tool results. Church baptismal registers are the primary source.

---

### Church records ⭐ Primary source for vital events

- Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985 (collection 1401638, 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons): **indexed + images** — broadest searchable Pennsylvania church record collection.
- Schuylkill County church records volume (007936751, 187 images, 1842–1895, English/German): **browse-only** — 0% indexed; bilingual — identify the record language before reading.
- **Catholic parish registers (coal-region specific):** Per the FamilySearch wiki ("Pennsylvania Coal Region Records"), many Catholic parishes were established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants. Baptismal registers are held by:
  - **Diocese of Scranton** — events from 1868 onward
  - **Diocese of Harrisburg** — events before 1868

---

### Census records

- Federal censuses for 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 cover all coal counties. The **1890 population schedules are mostly destroyed** — substitute with triennial state tax assessments.
- The **1880 census** is the first to record household member relationships — highest priority for proving family structure.
- The 1870 and 1900 censuses provide complementary evidence for families with children present (FamilySearch wiki).

---

### Probate records

- Schuylkill County probate volume (007936749, 412 images, 1851–1930): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania state probate volume (008120441, 1,180 images, 1683–1994): **browse-only** — 0% indexed.
- Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 893,214 records): **indexed + images**.

---

### Naturalization records ⭐ Critical for Irish immigrants

- Schuylkill County naturalization volume (007936750, 298 images, 1849–1915): **browse-only** — 0% indexed. Declarations of intent and petitions name country of origin; must be browsed image by image.
- Pennsylvania state naturalization volume (008120443, 351 images, 1790–1915, English/German): **15% name-indexed** — run a name search before browsing.
- **Pre-1906:** Records scattered among county Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts (FamilySearch wiki, "Pennsylvania Naturalization Records").
- **After September 1906:** Centralized in federal courts; NARA Philadelphia for eastern Pennsylvania.

---

### Land and deed records

- Schuylkill County deed records volume (007936752, 543 images, 1815–1900): **22% name-indexed** — partially searchable; the most accessible Schuylkill County volume by name search.

---

### Military records

- The Civil War (1861–1865) falls within the target period. Pennsylvania service records, pension files, and draft registrations are held at NARA. State adjutant general records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### Coal-region specialized indexes ⭐ Key for miner ancestors
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records")*

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** ~41,000 colliery workers named, drawn from company payroll books. Entries include occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin where stated — the most direct finding aid for Irish immigrant miners.
2. **Mine inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less useful for name lookups; use payroll-derived indexes first.
3. **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853:** List householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census.

---

### Tax records

- Triennial state assessments from 1853 cover coal-region residents; sometimes record nativity (FamilySearch wiki).
- Ancestry: Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 — pre-period, useful for establishing earlier family presence.

---

### Newspapers

- Coal-region papers (Pottsville, Scranton, Hazleton areas) carried obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices. Check Chronicling America and Newspapers.com for digitized runs.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this region | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (indexed) | Church and Town Records 1708–1985; County Marriages 1885–1950; Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; Probate Records 1683–1994; Death Certificates 1906–1968 | Free |
| FamilySearch (browse-only) | Schuylkill: naturalization 1849–1915 (298 images), church 1842–1895 (187 images, English/German), probate 1851–1930 (412 images), marriage 1870–1910 (94 images); PA state: death 1852–1968 (674 images); PA naturalization 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Federal Census – Schuylkill County; PA Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 | Subscription |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish baptismal registers, 1868 onward | Contact diocese |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic parish baptismal registers, pre-1868 | Contact diocese |
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, court records, naturalization dockets | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State records, military records, tax assessments | In-person / online |
| NARA Philadelphia | Post-1906 naturalizations; federal military records | In-person / research request |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1849–1915):** Digitized (298 images) but 0% indexed — browse image by image.
- **Schuylkill County church records (1842–1895):** Digitized (187 images) but 0% indexed; bilingual English/German.
- **Schuylkill County probate records (1851–1930):** Digitized (412 images) but 0% indexed.
- **Schuylkill County marriage records (1870–1910):** Digitized (94 images) but 0% indexed.
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index:** Described in the FamilySearch wiki but did not surface as a digitized FamilySearch collection — verify current online availability directly with FamilySearch or the relevant local repository.
- **Catholic parish registers (Diocese of Scranton / Diocese of Harrisburg):** May not be fully digitized; contact each diocese archive.

---

## Known record losses

- **1890 federal census:** Population schedules mostly destroyed nationwide. Substitute with triennial state tax assessments and church registers.
- No courthouse fires or major record losses for the coal counties were identified in tool results.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898).** ~41,000 colliery workers named with occupation and parish of origin — the most direct finding aid for Irish immigrant miners.
2. **Pre-1878 Lackawanna County events: search Luzerne County.** Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne in 1878; earlier records for the Scranton/Carbondale area are filed under Luzerne.
3. **Run naturalization records early.** Declarations and petitions name country of origin — often the only document confirming Irish birth. Try the 15%-indexed PA state naturalization volume first; then browse the Schuylkill County volume (298 images).
4. **Use the Diocese split for Catholic parish registers.** Diocese of Scranton (1868 onward) vs. Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868). Contact each archive for undigitized registers.
5. **Prioritize the 1880 census.** First federal census to record household member relationships — foundational for family structure.
6. **Triennial tax assessments substitute for 1890.** The 1853-onward assessments sometimes record nativity, useful for distinguishing Irish-born from American-born family members.
7. **Expect name anglicization and spelling variation.** Irish names were frequently anglicized. Search under both Irish and English forms and expect variation between mine employment records and church registers.
8. **Mine inspection/accident reports are by colliery, not by name.** Use payroll-derived indexes first for name lookups.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Vermont did not exist as a recognized jurisdiction during most of the late 1700s. The territory passed through three overlapping layers of authority before statehood:

- **New Hampshire Grants era (ca. 1749–1764):** Royal Governor Benning Wentworth issued more than 100 township grants in the region. These are the "New Hampshire Grants" that gave the territory its informal name.
- **New York jurisdiction (1764–1777):** Britain reassigned the territory to New York Colony, which refused to recognize the NH grants and attempted to issue its own patents. New York compiled the **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — documented in the FamilySearch wiki — which enumerated approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York disputed. Each entry lists the grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page, this is **the earliest systematic resident list for the future state**, predating any Vermont civil registration.
- **Republic of Vermont (1777–1791):** The territory declared independence from both NH and NY authority in 1777, established its own constitution, courts, and land records, and functioned as an independent republic until admitted to the Union.
- **Statehood:** Vermont was admitted as the **14th state on March 4, 1791**.

**FamilySearch's standardPlace** for Vermont (`Vermont, United States`) carries a dateRange of `+1791/` — meaning FamilySearch's jurisdiction formally begins at statehood. Records created before 1791 may be cataloged under New Hampshire, New York, or Vermont depending on which authority created them. This is the single most important research quirk for this period.

**Population:** No population data was returned by the FamilySearch population tool for this period. Vermont's population in 1791 was approximately 85,000 based on the first federal census.

**Economy and settlement:** Predominantly agricultural; small farming communities, subsistence and mixed farming, with some timber and mill industries. Settlement concentrated in the Connecticut River valley, Champlain valley, and along river corridors.

**Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (the dominant New England faith), Baptist, Methodist, and Episcopal congregations were established during the settlement period of the 1770s–1790s. Quaker settlements existed in some areas.

---

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 1749–1764 | New Hampshire Colony | Wentworth grants issued from Portsmouth, NH |
| 1764–1777 | New York Colony/State | Britain reassigned; NY contested all NH grants |
| 1777–1791 | Republic of Vermont | Self-governing; own courts, land records, constitution |
| 1791– | Vermont, United States | 14th state |

Vermont's own county structure was being established during the pre-statehood years. Bennington County was created in 1778, Windham in 1779, and others followed through the 1780s–1790s. **Records for events before a county existed are held by its parent jurisdiction** (the Republic of Vermont's state-level courts, or predecessor NH/NY records). For any town, determine which county it belonged to at the date of your event, because probate and court filings follow county jurisdiction.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began **1857** — per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki. There are **no civil birth, marriage, or death records for the pre-statehood period.**
- **Town clerk records:** The FamilySearch wiki notes that earlier town clerk records survive unevenly, with some reaching back to the **1770s**. Coverage is highly variable by town. Consult individual town clerk offices directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family Bibles, cemetery inscriptions, town proprietors' records, and newspaper notices are the primary substitutes for the pre-1857 gap.
- **Digitization status:** Specific FamilySearch collection listings for Vermont town clerk records could not be verified in this session (collections_search tool unavailable); check the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific town name.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal; scattered Quaker meetings.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists.
- **Survival:** Some congregations formed during the 1770s–1790s; record survival is uneven, and many early registers are fragmentary. Some have been transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Where held:** Local churches (if still active), Vermont Historical Society, denominational archives (e.g., the Congregational Library in Boston holds some New England records). FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records — check the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific town and denomination.
- **Access:** Likely microfilm or physical only for pre-1791 material; confirm via the FamilySearch Catalog.

### Census Records
- **1790 Federal Census:** Vermont was included in the first federal census (1790), even though statehood was finalized in March 1791. This is the **earliest federal enumeration** for the territory and lists heads of household with household member counts. **Indexed + images available** on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **No earlier federal census** exists for the territory.
- **Republic of Vermont enumerations:** The Republic may have conducted local enumerations for militia and tax purposes; consult Vermont State Archives.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** For the 1760s–1780s — before any census — Vermont town and county tax lists are the most reliable substitute enumeration. They document residents by name, often with property values.

### Land Records — THE PRIME SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD
Land records are the most important and richest record class for pre-statehood Vermont research.

- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Documented in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki as enumerating ~1,800 grantees of NH grants disputed by New York. Each entry: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, disputed-claim status. **The earliest systematic resident list for the future state.** Consult Vermont State Archives.
- **New Hampshire colonial grants (1749–1764):** Township proprietors' lists and individual grantee records are held at the New Hampshire State Archives and the NH Division of Records Management and Archives (Concord, NH). These may be the only documentary trace of settlers who arrived in the earliest wave.
- **New York patents (1764–1777):** For those who accepted New York authority during the dispute period. New York State Archives (Albany) holds these records.
- **Republic of Vermont land records (1777–1791):** Town proprietors' records and early deed books held at town clerk offices and Vermont State Archives. The FamilySearch wiki notes that **nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** that are otherwise difficult to access — these printed volumes are important finding aids.
- **Metes-and-bounds system:** Vermont is a state-land state; no federal land patents. Land ownership is documented through the town proprietors' records and county deed books.
- **Digitization status:** Specific collection and volume data could not be confirmed (tool unavailable); check the FamilySearch Catalog under the town or county name.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Probate courts** were established county by county as Vermont counties formed (Bennington 1778, Windham 1779, etc.). Wills, inventories, guardianships, and estate distributions for this period would be in county-level probate court files.
- **Republic of Vermont courts** also functioned as general courts of record before county-level organization was complete.
- **Where held:** Vermont Probate Court records for this era are held at the Vermont State Archives and in some cases at county courts. Check the Vermont State Archives online catalog.
- **Digitization status:** Cannot confirm from tool results; likely microfilm or physical access required for pre-1791 records.

### Military Records — HIGHLY PRODUCTIVE FOR THIS PERIOD
The pre-statehood period overlaps directly with the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), making military records an exceptionally valuable source.

- **Green Mountain Boys / Vermont militia:** Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys were organized from the disputed-grants settlers; rosters and muster rolls exist at the Vermont State Archives and through NARA.
- **Continental Army service:** Vermont men who served in Continental Army regiments are documented at NARA (Record Group 93). **Indexed + images** on Fold3.com.
- **Pension files:** Revolutionary War pension applications (filed after 1818 and 1832 acts) contain biographical narratives, family details, and residence histories — often the most detailed personal documents surviving for this era. **Indexed + images** on Fold3.com and Ancestry.com; also free on FamilySearch.
- **Bounty land warrants:** Issued for Revolutionary War service; document residence at time of application.
- **Vermont State Papers / adjutant general's records:** Published multi-volume *Vermont Revolutionary Rolls* document state-level militia service. Vermont State Archives holds additional unpublished rolls.

Vermont did not exist as a recognized jurisdiction for most of the late 1700s. The territory passed through **three overlapping layers of authority** before statehood — and each layer created its own records in its own archives:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Record Authority |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|
| ca. 1749–1764 | New Hampshire Colony | Gov. Wentworth's township grants |
| 1764–1777 | New York Colony/State | NY refused NH grants; issued own patents |
| 1777–1791 | Republic of Vermont | Own constitution, courts, land records |
| 1791– | Vermont, United States | 14th state, March 4, 1791 |

**The single most important jurisdictional quirk:** FamilySearch's standardPlace for Vermont carries a dateRange of `+1791/` — the jurisdiction formally begins at statehood. Records created before 1791 may be cataloged under New Hampshire, New York, or Vermont depending on which authority created them. Always search all three.

Vermont's county structure was being built during this period: Bennington County formed 1778, Windham 1779, and others through the 1780s–1790s. For probate and court records, identify which county existed at the date of your event — events before a county formed may be in Republic of Vermont state-level records.

**Population:** FamilySearch's population tool returned no data for this period. Vermont's population at the 1790 census was approximately 85,000. Settlement was concentrated in the Connecticut River valley, Lake Champlain valley, and river corridors.

**Economy:** Predominantly subsistence farming, timber, and mill industries. Small dispersed agricultural communities.

**Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, and scattered Quaker meetings — all being established during the 1770s–1790s settlement wave.

### 🏆 Land Records — THE PRIME SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD

Land records are the richest and most important record class for pre-statehood Vermont. Three separate archives hold relevant material:

**Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**
The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki documents this as **"the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."** Prepared under New York colonial authority, it enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration. Held at **Vermont State Archives**.

**New Hampshire colonial grants (1749–1764)**
Governor Benning Wentworth's township grants and individual grantee records. Held at **New Hampshire State Archives, Concord, NH**. These are often the only documentary trace of the earliest wave of settlers.

**New York patents (1764–1777)**
For settlers who accepted New York authority. Held at **New York State Archives, Albany, NY**.

**Republic of Vermont records (1777–1791)**
Town proprietors' records and early deed books. Held at **Vermont State Archives** and individual **town clerk offices**.

- **New Hampshire Grants era (ca. 1749–1764):** Royal Governor Benning Wentworth issued more than 100 township grants in the region.
- **New York jurisdiction (1764–1777):** Britain reassigned the territory to New York Colony, which refused to recognize the NH grants and compiled the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — ~1,800 grantees of NH grants, listing grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, this is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
- **Republic of Vermont (1777–1791):** Declared independence; own constitution, courts, and land records.
- **Statehood:** 14th state admitted March 4, 1791.

FamilySearch's standardPlace for Vermont (dateRange +1791/) formally begins at statehood. Pre-statehood records may be cataloged under New Hampshire, New York, or Vermont.

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Jurisdiction |
|--------|-------------|
| 1749–1764 | New Hampshire Colony |
| 1764–1777 | New York Colony/State |
| 1777–1791 | Republic of Vermont |
| 1791– | Vermont, United States |

Vermont county formation began 1778 (Bennington), 1779 (Windham), and continued through the 1780s–1790s. Records follow the county that existed at the event date.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records
- **No civil records for this period.** Statewide registration began 1857 (per FamilySearch wiki).
- Town clerk records survive unevenly, some from the 1770s; consult town clerk offices directly.
- Substitutes: church records, family Bibles, cemetery inscriptions, town proprietors' records, newspapers.

### Land Records — Prime Source
- Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule: ~1,800 grantees, held at Vermont State Archives.
- NH colonial grants: NH State Archives, Concord.
- NY patents (disputed territory): NY State Archives, Albany.
- Republic of Vermont records from 1777: Vermont State Archives and town clerk offices.
- Town histories (1860–1900) reprint colonial-era proprietors' records — many free on Google Books/Internet Archive.

### Church Records
- Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, Quaker.
- Some records from 1770s–1790s; survival uneven.
- Held at local churches, Vermont Historical Society, denominational archives.
- Check FamilySearch Catalog by town and denomination.

### Census Records
- First federal census: 1790 (indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry).
- No earlier federal census.
- Tax lists (late 1770s onward) substitute for pre-1790 enumeration.

### Military Records
- Revolutionary War (1775–1783): pension files, service records, muster rolls.
- Green Mountain Boys rosters at Vermont State Archives.
- Continental Army records at NARA; indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- Pension files (post-1818/1832) contain rich biographical narratives.

### Probate and Court Records
- County probate courts formed as counties organized from 1778 onward.
- Vermont State Archives; some county court offices.

### Cemetery Records
- Town burying grounds and church cemeteries with stones from 1770s–1790s.
- Find A Grave and BillionGraves index many Vermont inscriptions.
- DAR transcriptions published in Vermont genealogical journals.

### Tax Records
- Town and county tax lists from late 1770s onward.
- Primary census substitute for 1760–1790 gap.
- Vermont State Archives and town clerk offices.

### Newspaper Records
- Vermont Gazette (Bennington, 1783) among earliest; coverage thin pre-1791.
- Newspapers.com for digitized early Vermont papers.

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 census; Rev. War pensions; microfilmed VT holdings (check Catalog) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 census; Rev. War records; some VT vital/land records | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Rev. War service, pensions, muster rolls | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | VT cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Early VT newspapers | Subscription |
| Google Books / Internet Archive | VT town histories (1860–1900) with reprinted proprietors' records | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (VSARA), Montpelier | Republic of VT records, early land/probate/court records, military rolls |
| Vermont Historical Society, Barre | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections |
| Town clerk offices | Deeds, proprietors' records, early vital records, tax lists |
| NH State Archives, Concord | NH colonial grant records (Wentworth grants) |
| NY State Archives, Albany | NY patents for disputed VT territory, 1764–1777 |
| NARA | Rev. War service/pension records, 1790 census |

## Records NOT Online
- Town clerk vital records (pre-1857): mostly physical or microfilm
- Town/county tax lists: Vermont State Archives and town offices
- Republic of Vermont court/legislative records: Vermont State Archives
- NH colonial grant records: NH State Archives
- NY patents for VT territory: NY State Archives
- Early church registers: check FamilySearch Catalog

## Research Tips
1. Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
2. FamilySearch's Vermont jurisdiction starts at 1791 — also search under New Hampshire and check Republic of Vermont records.
3. Town histories (1860–1900) reprint colonial proprietors' records; many are free on Google Books.
4. No civil vital records for this period — pivot to church records, tax lists, cemetery inscriptions.
5. Revolutionary War pension files are often the richest biographical source for men born ca. 1740–1765.
6. Tax lists substitute for the missing 1760s–1780s census.
7. Search NH, NY, and VT archives for land records — an ancestor may appear in all three.
8. County formation determines probate/court filing location — identify the county that existed at the event date.
